chapters.n: The Bible opens by declaring that everything begins with God. Latter-day Saint scripture adds that God worked through His Son, and that “created” here means organizing existing matter rather than making something out of nothing.

f.g: Hebrew bara’ — to shape or form; used in the Bible only of God’s work. Abraham 4:1 renders it “organized and formed.”

chapters.n: Before God’s ordering work, the earth was shapeless, empty, and dark, covered by deep waters. Yet the Spirit of God was already present, hovering over it like a bird over its nest, ready to bring forth life.

f.g: Hebrew tohu wa-bohu — formless and empty. Days 1–3 give the earth form; days 4–6 fill it.
Hebrew raḥaf — to hover or brood, as a bird over its young (compare Deuteronomy 32:11).

chapters.n: God simply speaks, and light appears. This shows the power of His word. Christians have long seen a link to Jesus Christ, who is called the Word and the Light of the world.

God looks at His work and calls it good, a refrain repeated throughout the chapter. Separating light from darkness is the first of several acts of dividing and ordering that turn chaos into a home for life.

f.g: Separating and ordering is a key theme: light from darkness, waters from waters, sea from land.

chapters.n: Naming something showed authority over it. The Hebrew day begins at evening, which is why the text says “evening and morning.” Latter-day Saint scripture treats each creative “day” as a period of time rather than necessarily 24 hours.

f.g: Abraham 4:5 calls it “the first, or the beginning, of that which they called day and night”; the Abraham account speaks of creative “times.”

chapters.n: On the second day God makes an expanse, the sky, which separates waters above from waters below. To ancient eyes the sky looked like a great dome holding back rain clouds.

f.g: Hebrew raqiaʿ — something beaten or spread out; an expanse. Abraham 4:6 uses “expanse.”

chapters.n: The command is carried out exactly as spoken. “It was so” stresses that God’s word is always fulfilled. In the Abraham account, the Gods watch “until they obeyed,” showing creation responding to divine direction.

God names the expanse “Heaven,” meaning the sky. Notably, the second day is the only one where the text does not call the work “good”—many readers think the waters’ work was not finished until day three.

f.g: Here the visible sky, not the dwelling place of God.

chapters.n: On the third day the waters gather into one place and dry ground appears. A world fit for plants, animals, and people is being prepared step by step.
God names the land and seas and declares them good. The land is now ready to bear life, and God’s approval is stamped on it.

f.g: Hebrew yammim — the great waters, which ancient peoples often feared; here they are simply part of God’s ordered world.

chapters.n: God commands the earth to produce plants. Each one carries its own seed and reproduces “after his kind,” a built-in order that lets life continue and multiply on its own.

f.g: “His” is older English for “its.” Each kind reproduces according to its own pattern.

chapters.n: The earth obeys and becomes green with life. Seed-bearing plants and fruit trees will later feed both animals and people, showing God’s care in providing for His children before they arrive.

f.g: Plants in general, especially grain and vegetables—not just seasonings.

chapters.n: The third day closes. It contained two creative acts: forming dry land and clothing it with plants.

f.g: Days 1–3 create spaces (light, sky and sea, land); days 4–6 fill those spaces.

chapters.n: On the fourth day God places lights in the sky. They mark time—signs, seasons, days, and years—which later governs Israel’s calendar of feasts and sacred days.

f.g: Hebrew moʿadim — appointed times, the same word used for Israel’s holy festivals.

chapters.n: These lights have a practical purpose: to shine on the earth. Everything in creation is aimed at making the earth a good place for life.

f.w: to give light upon the earth

chapters.n: God makes the sun and moon, here called simply the greater and lesser lights, and almost in passing, the stars. Many neighboring peoples worshipped these bodies; Genesis presents them as God’s creations, not gods.
God sets the lights in their place in the sky. Their job is to serve the earth by giving light.

f.g: Placed or appointed—the lights have positions and roles assigned by God.

chapters.n: The sun and moon “rule” day and night, but only as servants doing what God assigned. Their ordered motion reflects God’s orderly creation.
The fourth day ends with the heavens now furnished with lights.

f.g: Day four fills the space made on day one (light and darkness).

chapters.n: On the fifth day the waters swarm with life and birds fill the sky. Life now moves and breathes, filling the spaces made on day two.

f.g: Swarming creatures—things that teem in great numbers.

chapters.n: God creates sea creatures large and small and every kind of bird. The great sea creatures, feared by ancient peoples as monsters, are shown to be simply part of God’s good creation.

f.g: Hebrew tannin — great sea creatures or sea monsters, not only whales.

chapters.n: God blesses the creatures to multiply. This is the first blessing in the Bible, and it is a blessing of life and increase.
The fifth day closes with sea and sky full of living things.

f.g: Day five fills the spaces separated on day two (waters below, sky above).

chapters.n: On the sixth day the land brings forth animals—livestock, small creeping creatures, and wild animals—each reproducing according to its kind.

f.g: In KJV English, domestic animals and livestock in general.

chapters.n: God makes every kind of land animal and approves of it. The stage is now set for the crowning act of creation.

f.g: Small ground creatures—insects, reptiles, and the like.

chapters.n: The tone changes: God speaks with others—“Let us.” Latter-day Saints understand this as the Father speaking with His Son and other heavenly beings. Humans are made in God’s image and given care of the earth.

f.w: in our image, after our likeness

f.g: Responsible stewardship—ruling as God would rule, with care (compare D&C 104:13-17).

chapters.n: The poetic repetition emphasizes the point: men and women alike are created in God’s image. Both sexes together reflect the divine. Latter-day Saints teach that we are literally spirit children of Heavenly Parents.

f.w: male and female created he them

chapters.n: God blesses the first man and woman and gives them their first commandment: have children and care for the earth. Family and stewardship are woven into human purpose from the start.

f.g: Here simply “fill”—not “refill.”
To bring under control and make productive; to cultivate.

chapters.n: God provides food for humanity: seed-bearing plants and fruit. He is a generous Father who prepares for His children’s needs.

f.g: In KJV English, “meat” means food of any kind, not just animal flesh.

chapters.n: Animals, too, receive green plants for food. The picture is of a peaceful world where every creature is provided for.
God surveys everything and declares it “very good”—the only time this stronger phrase appears. The creation, including the human body, is good. This ends the sixth day.

The creation is complete. The “host” means everything that fills the heavens and earth—stars, creatures, and all. The chapter division here interrupts the creation story, which really ends at verse 3.

f.g: A great company or army; here, all the things that fill heaven and earth.

chapters.n: God “rests” on the seventh day—not because He is tired, but because the work is finished. His rest sets a pattern for His children to stop their labors and turn to Him.

f.g: Hebrew shavat — to stop or cease; the root of “Sabbath.”

chapters.n: God blesses the seventh day and makes it holy. This is the root of the Sabbath, a weekly reminder that time itself belongs to God and that creation is His gift.

f.g: Made holy; set apart for a sacred purpose.

chapters.n: A new section begins, using a new name for God: “the LORD God.” In KJV small capitals, LORD stands for the sacred name Jehovah, whom Latter-day Saints understand to be the premortal Jesus Christ.

f.g: Hebrew toledot — “account” or “family history.” This phrase marks new sections throughout Genesis (5:1; 6:9; 10:1; 11:10).
Hebrew YHWH Elohim. Printed LORD in capitals to signal the divine name.

chapters.n: Plants did not yet grow in the fields, since there was no rain and no one to farm. The book of Moses explains that God first created all things spiritually before they existed naturally on the earth.

f.w: before it was in the earth

f.g: To plow and work the soil.

chapters.n: Water rises from the ground to moisten the land, preparing it for life even before rain.

f.g: Hebrew ’ed — perhaps a spring or stream rising from the ground; the meaning is uncertain.

chapters.n: God shapes the man from earth like a potter and breathes life into him. Body and spirit together make a “living soul,” an idea restoration scripture makes explicit: the spirit and body are the soul of man.

f.g: Hebrew yatsar — to shape, as a potter shapes clay.
Wordplay: ’adam (man) is formed from ’adamah (ground).

chapters.n: God plants a garden in Eden, toward the east, and places the man there. The garden is a place of God’s presence—like a first temple.

f.g: The name likely means “delight” or “pleasure.”

chapters.n: The garden is beautiful and full of food. In its center stand two special trees: the tree of life and the tree of knowledge of good and evil. These two trees will set up the choice that follows.

f.w: the tree of knowledge of good and evil

chapters.n: A single river flows out of Eden and divides into four. Water flowing from God’s presence becomes a recurring image of life-giving blessing.

f.w: a river went out of Eden

f.g: Headwaters or branches of a river.

chapters.n: The first river, Pison, winds around the land of Havilah, known for its gold. Its location is uncertain today.

f.g: Goes around; winds through.
A region probably in or near Arabia (compare Genesis 10:7, 29).

chapters.n: Havilah’s riches are listed: fine gold, a fragrant resin, and precious stones. Such materials later adorn the tabernacle and the high priest’s clothing.

f.g: Probably a fragrant, pale resin (compare Numbers 11:7).

chapters.n: The second river, Gihon, flows around “Ethiopia,” here translating Cush. The exact region intended is debated.

f.g: Hebrew Cush, which can mean Ethiopia/Nubia or a region in Mesopotamia.

chapters.n: The third river, Hiddekel, is the Tigris, and the fourth is the Euphrates—both well-known rivers of Mesopotamia. These names root the story in a real geography.

f.g: The Tigris River (compare Daniel 10:4).

chapters.n: Adam is given work in paradise: to tend and protect the garden. Meaningful labor is part of God’s design for humanity, not just a result of the Fall.

f.w: to dress it and to keep it
f.g: To work and to guard it. The same Hebrew verbs later describe priests serving and guarding the tabernacle (Numbers 3:7-8).

chapters.n: God speaks to Adam with great generosity first: every tree is available. The commandment that follows comes within a setting of abundance.

f.g: Without restriction.

chapters.n: Only one tree is forbidden, and eating it will bring death. The book of Moses adds that God told Adam he could still choose for himself—agency is part of the plan.

f.g: Abraham 5:13 notes this was reckoned by the Lord’s time, in which a day may be a thousand years.

chapters.n: For the first time something is “not good”: being alone. God plans a partner who corresponds to the man and stands beside him as an equal help.

f.g: “Meet” = suitable or fitting. Hebrew ʿezer kenegdo — a helper corresponding to him, “face to face.” ʿEzer is also used of God helping Israel.

chapters.n: God brings the animals to Adam to name them. Naming shows Adam’s God-given stewardship and also prepares him to notice what is missing.

f.w: to see what he would call them
f.g: God gives Adam real responsibility and respects his choices.

chapters.n: Adam names every animal, but none is a true partner for him. The search highlights how unique the woman will be.

f.g: Here becomes a personal name; Hebrew ’adam also means “man” or “mankind.”

chapters.n: God puts Adam into a deep sleep and takes part of his side. Adam does not witness the woman’s creation; she is entirely God’s work.

f.g: Hebrew tselaʿ — side. The image suggests the woman stands at the man’s side, neither above nor below him. President Spencer W. Kimball taught that the rib account is figurative.

chapters.n: God fashions the woman and brings her to the man, as a father might present a bride. This is the first marriage, performed by God Himself.
Adam bursts into the Bible’s first poetry with joy: at last, someone like him! The Hebrew wordplay ’ishah (woman) and ’ish (man) shows their deep kinship.

f.w: bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh
f.g: A Hebrew idiom for close family relationship (compare 2 Samuel 5:1).
Hebrew ’ishah, from ’ish, “man.”

chapters.n: The narrator draws a lasting lesson: marriage creates a new, primary bond. Jesus quoted this verse to teach that God joins husband and wife.

f.g: A complete union of life—physical, emotional, and spiritual.

chapters.n: In their innocence the man and woman feel no shame. This sets up the change that comes in the next chapter after the Fall.

f.g: Hebrew ʿarumim — a wordplay with the “subtil” (ʿarum) serpent in 3:1.

chapters.n: A crafty serpent questions God’s command, twisting it to sound harsher than it was. The book of Moses reveals that Satan was speaking through the serpent, seeking to destroy God’s plan.

f.g: Subtle—crafty, cunning, shrewd.

chapters.n: Eve corrects the serpent: they may eat from the garden’s trees. She knows God has been generous.

f.g: Eve’s reply shows she understood God’s command well.

chapters.n: Eve names the one forbidden tree and adds “neither shall ye touch it,” which God did not say in chapter 2. Some readers see a protective fence around the command; others see the rule growing stricter in her mind.
The serpent flatly contradicts God. This is the first lie in scripture, and Jesus later called the devil “a liar, and the father of it.”

Satan mixes truth with deception. Eating would open their eyes and bring knowledge of good and evil—God later confirms this in verse 22—but Satan hides the cost and paints God as withholding good things.

f.w: ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil

chapters.n: Eve sees that the fruit is good, beautiful, and promises wisdom, and she eats; Adam eats too. Latter-day Saints view this as a choice that opened mortality and the way to eternal progress, though it brought real consequences.

f.g: Eve was drawn by a desire for wisdom, not mere appetite.

f.w: she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat

chapters.n: Their eyes are opened, and they suddenly feel exposed. They try to cover themselves with fig leaves—a human attempt to hide shame that God will soon replace with His own covering.

f.g: Fig leaves are large but brittle—a poor, temporary covering.
Loincloths or coverings for the waist.

chapters.n: God comes walking in the garden in the evening breeze, but Adam and Eve hide among the trees. The garden that was a place of fellowship becomes a place of hiding.

f.w: in the cool of the day
f.g: Literally “in the wind (or spirit) of the day”—the breezy evening hours.

chapters.n: God calls, “Where art thou?” He knows where Adam is; the question invites Adam to come out and own what he has done. God seeks His children even after they fall.
Adam admits fear and shame. Before, God’s voice brought joy; now it brings fear. Sin changes how we feel in God’s presence.
God asks two pointed questions, giving Adam the chance to confess honestly.

f.g: God’s questions are a gentle form of judgment that invites honesty.

chapters.n: Adam blames Eve—and indirectly God, who “gave” her. The blame game begins.

f.w: The woman whom thou gavest to be with me
f.g: Adam shifts responsibility to both Eve and God.

chapters.n: Eve says the serpent deceived her. Her answer is more honest about deception, but she too points elsewhere.

f.g: Deceived or tricked.

chapters.n: God curses the serpent first. Crawling and “eating dust” picture deep humiliation and defeat.

This is often called the first gospel promise. There will be ongoing conflict between Satan and humanity, but a descendant of the woman will crush the serpent’s head while suffering a wound to the heel—a prophecy of Jesus Christ’s victory.

f.g: A fatal, crushing blow, compared to the serpent’s lesser strike at the heel.

chapters.n: Eve’s life will now include pain in bearing children, yet also the privilege of motherhood. Her relationship with her husband will also face new strains in a fallen world.

f.g: Hebrew ʿitsavon — pain, toil, hard labor; the same word is used of Adam’s toil in verse 17.
Latter-day Saint leaders have taught that the sense is to preside in love and righteousness, as equal partners, not to dominate.

chapters.n: The ground is cursed “for thy sake”—for Adam’s benefit. Hard work in a resistant world will help him grow. Mortal life will be a place of effort and learning.

f.g: Can mean both “because of you” and “for your benefit.”
Listened to and obeyed.

chapters.n: Weeds and thorns will make farming difficult. Thorns later become a symbol of the curse that Christ bore when He wore a crown of thorns.
Life will now require sweaty labor, and death will come: the body returns to the earth it came from. Physical death enters the world through the Fall.

f.w: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return

chapters.n: Right after hearing about death, Adam names his wife Eve, “living.” It is an act of hope: through her, life will continue and the promised Seed will come.

f.g: Hebrew Ḥawwah, related to ḥay, “living.”

chapters.n: God Himself makes garments of skins to clothe them, replacing their fig leaves. An animal’s life was apparently given, and many see here a foreshadowing of Christ’s atoning sacrifice that covers sin.

f.g: The Hebrew word for “atonement” (kippur) has a root linked to covering.

chapters.n: Having gained knowledge of good and evil, Adam and Eve must not eat of the tree of life and live forever in their fallen state. Alma explains they needed a probationary time to repent.

f.g: God speaks again in the plural, as in Genesis 1:26.

chapters.n: God sends Adam out of Eden to work the ground. Mortal life on the earth now begins.
Cherubim—heavenly guardians—and a flaming sword block the way back to the tree of life. Yet the way is guarded, not destroyed; through Christ, the path back to God’s presence is opened again.

f.g: “Cherubim” is already plural in Hebrew. Images of cherubim later guard the ark of the covenant in the temple.

f.w: the way of the tree of life

chapters.n: Outside Eden, Adam and Eve’s family begins. Eve’s joyful words may express hope that this son is the promised Seed. The book of Moses adds that they already had other sons and daughters before Cain.

f.g: A Hebrew idiom for marital intimacy.
Sounds like Hebrew qanah, “to get” or “acquire.”

chapters.n: Abel is born, and the brothers take up the two great livelihoods: shepherding and farming. Abel’s name means “breath” or “vapor,” perhaps hinting at his short life.

f.g: Hebrew Hevel — breath, vapor, something fleeting (the same word as “vanity” in Ecclesiastes).

chapters.n: Cain brings produce from his fields as an offering. The book of Moses explains that Adam had been commanded to offer the firstlings of the flock as a symbol of the Savior’s sacrifice.

f.g: Literally “at the end of days”—after some time had passed.

chapters.n: Abel brings the best: firstborn lambs and their fat portions. The Lord accepts him and his offering. Hebrews says Abel offered “by faith,” pointing to the Lamb of God.

f.g: The firstborn of the flock—the best and most valuable.
Looked with favor on; accepted.

chapters.n: Cain’s offering is not accepted. Instead of seeking to improve, he becomes furious and sullen. Restoration scripture says Cain made his offering at Satan’s urging and loved Satan more than God.

f.g: His face fell—he looked downcast and angry.

chapters.n: The Lord lovingly reaches out to Cain with questions, inviting him to examine his heart before anger becomes sin.

f.g: Very angry.

chapters.n: God offers hope and a warning: do right and you will be accepted, but sin is crouching at your door like a wild animal, eager to master you—you must master it.

f.g: “Lieth” translates a word for a crouching animal waiting to pounce.

chapters.n: Cain lures his brother into the field and kills him—the first murder. The book of Moses reveals that Cain had made a secret pact with Satan to murder for gain.

f.g: Ancient versions add, “Let us go out into the field.”

chapters.n: God asks Cain where Abel is, again inviting confession. Cain lies and sneers, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” The rest of scripture answers: yes, we are responsible for one another.
Abel’s blood “cries out” from the ground for justice. God hears innocent suffering even when no human witness does.

f.w: crieth unto me from the ground

chapters.n: Cain is cursed from the very ground that received his brother’s blood. Adam’s ground was cursed for his benefit; Cain himself is now cursed.
The farmer will no longer reap good harvests. Cain will be a restless wanderer without a settled home.

f.g: A wanderer and drifter, constantly on the move.

chapters.n: Cain complains that his punishment is too great. His concern is for himself, not grief for his brother or his sin.

f.g: Hebrew ʿawon can mean both “iniquity” and “its punishment.”

chapters.n: Cain fears being hidden from God’s face and killed by others. Being cut off from God’s presence is the heaviest part of his sentence.

f.w: from thy face shall I be hid

chapters.n: Even in judgment, God shows mercy: He places a protective mark on Cain so no one will take vengeance on him. Scripture does not say what the mark was.

f.g: Seven times over—full, complete vengeance.
A sign of protection; its nature is not described.

chapters.n: Cain leaves God’s presence and settles in Nod, east of Eden. Moving “east” in Genesis often signals moving away from God.

f.g: Means “wandering”—fitting for a fugitive.

chapters.n: Cain’s line builds the first city, named after his son Enoch. This Enoch is not the righteous Enoch of chapter 5 and the book of Moses.

f.g: Not the prophet Enoch (Genesis 5:18-24), who descended from Seth.

chapters.n: Cain’s family line continues for several generations, ending in Lamech.

f.g: Not the same as Noah’s father Lamech of Genesis 5:25-31.

chapters.n: Lamech takes two wives, the first recorded case of plural marriage, appearing in a family line marked by pride and violence.

f.g: Means perhaps “ornament”; Zillah perhaps “shade.”

chapters.n: Lamech’s son Jabal starts the herding way of life, living in tents and keeping livestock.

f.g: Founder or originator of a way of life.

chapters.n: Jubal is the founder of music. The line of Cain develops culture and skill, showing that talent is a gift even where faith is lacking.

f.g: A pipe or flute, not the modern organ.

chapters.n: Tubal-cain begins metalworking, crafting tools and perhaps weapons. Naamah, his sister, is named, which is unusual in a genealogy.

f.g: A forger or teacher of all craftsmen.
In the KJV usually copper or bronze.

chapters.n: Lamech boasts to his wives in a violent poem about killing a man who merely wounded him. Restoration scripture says he killed to protect the secrets of a combination begun by Cain.

f.w: I have slain a man to my wounding

chapters.n: Lamech twists God’s protection of Cain into a boast of unlimited revenge. Jesus later reverses this, teaching His disciples to forgive “seventy times seven.”
Adam and Eve receive another son, Seth, through whom the righteous line will continue. Eve sees him as God’s gift replacing Abel.

f.g: Sounds like Hebrew shat, “appointed” or “granted.”

chapters.n: Through Seth’s son Enos, people begin to worship and call on the Lord’s name. The book of Moses teaches that Adam’s family was taught the gospel from the beginning.

f.w: call upon the name of the LORD

f.g: Hebrew ’Enosh, “man” or “mortal.”

chapters.n: A new section begins: the family record of Adam. It reminds us that humans were made in God’s likeness. The book of Moses mentions that Adam’s family kept a “book of remembrance.”

f.w: the book of the generations of Adam

chapters.n: Men and women together are blessed by God and called “Adam,” meaning humankind. Both share the dignity of being created by God.

f.g: Hebrew ’adam can mean “mankind” as well as the first man’s name.

chapters.n: Seth is born “in Adam’s image,” echoing how Adam was made in God’s image. The family likeness passes from God to Adam to Seth, linking all generations to God.

f.w: in his own likeness, after his image

chapters.n: Adam lives many more years and has many children. Genealogies like this show that God’s blessing to multiply was being fulfilled.

f.g: Only key sons are named, but large families are implied.

chapters.n: Adam dies at 930, fulfilling the warning that death would come. Shortly before his death, restoration scripture says, Adam gathered his righteous posterity at Adam-ondi-Ahman and blessed them.
Seth becomes father to Enos. The repeated pattern—age at fatherhood, years after, total years—gives the chapter a steady, rhythmic feel.
Seth continues to live and raise a large family for centuries after Enos’s birth.

f.g: These long lifespans are a striking feature of the pre-Flood generations.

chapters.n: Seth dies at 912. The refrain “and he died” echoes through the chapter, reminding readers that mortality now touches every life.

f.g: Repeated eight times in this chapter—with one striking exception (verse 24).

chapters.n: Enos fathers Cainan. Doctrine and Covenants 107 adds that these patriarchs received priesthood ordination in their generations.
Enos lives on for centuries, raising a large family.

f.g: Became the father of; sometimes means ancestor of.

chapters.n: Enos dies at 905.

f.g: Total years of Enos’s life.

chapters.n: Cainan fathers Mahalaleel, whose name praises God—hinting at the faith of this family line.

f.g: Means “praise of God.”

chapters.n: Cainan lives on and has many children.

f.g: Years Cainan lived after Mahalaleel’s birth.

chapters.n: Cainan dies at 910.

f.g: Cainan’s total lifespan.

chapters.n: Mahalaleel fathers Jared.

f.g: Means “descent” or “coming down.”

chapters.n: Mahalaleel lives on and raises sons and daughters.

f.g: Years Mahalaleel lived after Jared’s birth.

chapters.n: Mahalaleel dies at 895.

f.w: eight hundred ninety and five years
f.g: Mahalaleel’s total lifespan.

chapters.n: Jared fathers Enoch, one of the greatest prophets of the early world. The book of Moses records Enoch’s ministry in rich detail.
Jared lives on and raises a large family. The book of Moses says Jared taught Enoch “in all the ways of God.”
Jared lives 962 years, the second-longest lifespan recorded.

f.w: nine hundred sixty and two years
f.g: Only Methuselah lived longer (verse 27).

chapters.n: Enoch fathers Methuselah at sixty-five.

f.g: The name may mean “man of the spear” or “man sent forth.”

chapters.n: Enoch “walked with God”—a lovely phrase for living in close, daily fellowship with the Lord. He did so while raising a family.

f.g: Lived in close companionship and obedience with God.

chapters.n: Enoch’s 365 years is much shorter than his relatives’ lifespans, but his life does not end in ordinary death.

f.w: three hundred sixty and five years

chapters.n: Instead of “and he died,” Enoch simply “was not; for God took him.” Restoration scripture teaches that Enoch and his city of Zion were taken into heaven because of their righteousness.
Methuselah fathers Lamech.

f.g: A different man from the violent Lamech of Cain’s line (4:18-24).

chapters.n: Methuselah lives on for centuries and raises a large family. The book of Moses says he was not taken with Enoch so that God’s covenant through his line could be fulfilled.
Methuselah lives 969 years, the longest life in the Bible. By the chapter’s numbers, he died in the year of the Flood.

f.w: nine hundred sixty and nine years
f.g: The oldest age recorded in scripture.

chapters.n: Lamech fathers a son at 182.

f.g: The son is named in the next verse.

chapters.n: Lamech names his son Noah, hoping he will bring relief from the hard toil caused by the curse on the ground. Noah will indeed bring rest and a new beginning.

f.g: Sounds like Hebrew nuaḥ, “rest,” and is linked here to naḥam, “comfort.”

f.w: the ground which the LORD hath cursed

chapters.n: Lamech lives on and raises other children.

f.w: five hundred ninety and five years
f.g: Years Lamech lived after Noah’s birth.

chapters.n: Lamech dies at 777—a number some see as fitting, in contrast to the boastful “seventy and sevenfold” of Cain’s Lamech.

f.w: seven hundred seventy and seven years

chapters.n: Noah becomes father to Shem, Ham, and Japheth, the three sons through whom the earth will be repopulated after the Flood. The stage is set for the next great chapter.
As the human family grows, the story turns toward a crisis. The book of Moses adds that Noah and his sons had daughters too, setting up the marriages described next.

The “sons of God” marry the “daughters of men” simply because they are attractive. Restoration scripture explains these were descendants of Noah who married outside the covenant into a wicked society, despite warnings.

f.g: Many interpretations exist. The book of Moses identifies covenant-keeping people, and notes that wicked men also falsely claimed the title.
Beautiful.

chapters.n: God says His Spirit will not keep striving with people forever. A limit of 120 years is set—perhaps a final period for repentance before the Flood.

f.w: My spirit shall not always strive with man

f.g: Likely the time left before the Flood, though some read it as a new limit on human lifespan.

chapters.n: This era had “giants”—mighty, famous men. Fame and strength, however, came with violence and corruption, as the next verses show.

f.g: Hebrew nephilim — perhaps “fallen ones”; powerful, violent men. Compare Numbers 13:33.
Famous men; literally “men of name.”

chapters.n: God sees that human wickedness has become total: even people’s thoughts are constantly evil. Sin begins in the heart and imagination before it becomes action.

f.w: every imagination of the thoughts of his heart

chapters.n: God grieves deeply over humanity. He is not a distant force but a Father whose heart aches at His children’s choices. The JST says it was Noah who “repented” or grieved.

f.g: Hebrew naḥam — to be sorry or grieve. The JST/Moses 8:25 reads “it repented Noah, and his heart was pained.”

chapters.n: God announces that He will wipe out life on the earth. The destruction of creation mirrors the creation account in reverse—people, beasts, creeping things, and birds.
One man stands out. “Grace” here means God’s favor. Noah’s righteousness does not earn the Flood’s escape so much as respond to God’s gracious choice of him.

f.g: Favor; kindness freely given.

chapters.n: Noah’s story begins. He is just, whole-hearted, and like Enoch, “walked with God.” “Perfect” means complete or blameless, not flawless.

f.g: Hebrew tamim — whole, complete, blameless; spiritually mature.

chapters.n: Noah’s three sons are named again, as the family through whom humanity will continue.
The earth is corrupt and full of violence. In Hebrew, violence (ḥamas) means cruel injustice and bloodshed that ruins society.

f.g: Hebrew ḥamas — violent wrongdoing, cruelty, injustice.

chapters.n: God looks and sees that “all flesh” has ruined its way. The world He called “very good” has been spoiled by human choices.

f.g: Ruined, spoiled. The same Hebrew verb is translated “destroy” in verse 13—God brings an end to what people had already ruined.

chapters.n: God tells Noah that the end has come for this violent world. Moses 8 adds that Noah had preached repentance for years, but the people would not listen.

f.w: The end of all flesh is come before me

chapters.n: God gives Noah detailed instructions for a great boat with rooms, sealed inside and out with pitch. The same Hebrew word for “ark” is used for the basket that saved baby Moses.

f.g: Hebrew tevah — a box or chest; used elsewhere only for Moses’ basket (Exodus 2:3).
An unknown type of wood, perhaps cypress.
Tar or bitumen for waterproofing.

chapters.n: The ark is huge—about 450 feet long, 75 feet wide, and 45 feet high. Its proportions are those of a stable barge built to float, not to sail.

f.g: A cubit is about 18 inches (45 cm), the length from elbow to fingertip.

chapters.n: The ark has an opening for light near the top, one door in the side, and three decks. Like the Jaredite barges, God guides the design for survival.

f.g: Hebrew tsohar — an opening for light, perhaps a roof gap running around the top.

chapters.n: God Himself will bring the Flood. The emphatic “I, even I” makes clear that this is God’s judgment, not random disaster.

f.g: Emphatic repetition stressing God’s direct action.

chapters.n: This is the first use of the word “covenant” in the Bible. God promises to preserve Noah and his family. Covenants become the backbone of God’s relationship with His people.

f.g: A binding, sacred agreement initiated by God.

chapters.n: Noah is to bring pairs of every kind of creature to keep life alive. The ark is a floating preservation of creation.
Birds, animals, and creeping things will “come unto” Noah—God will lead them to the ark.

f.g: The animals come to Noah; he does not have to hunt them down.

chapters.n: Noah must store food for his family and the animals. Faith includes practical preparation.

f.w: take thou unto thee of all food

chapters.n: Noah obeys completely. His faith is shown by building an ark for a flood no one could yet see.

f.w: according to all that God commanded him

chapters.n: The Lord invites Noah and his household into the ark. The word “come” is warm: God is calling Noah to safety, not simply sending him off.

f.w: Come thou and all thy house into the ark

chapters.n: Noah is to take seven pairs of “clean” animals—those later fit for sacrifice and food—and one pair of the others. The extra clean animals allow for offerings after the Flood.

f.g: Animals acceptable for sacrifice; later defined in the law of Moses.
Possibly seven pairs, or seven individuals; Hebrew is ambiguous.

chapters.n: Birds also come by sevens so that every kind survives to repopulate the earth.

f.g: To preserve offspring—that life may continue.

chapters.n: One last week of waiting, then forty days and nights of rain. Forty in scripture often marks a period of testing or renewal.

f.g: Forty recurs in times of trial: Moses on Sinai, Israel in the wilderness, Jesus in the desert.
Living thing or being.

chapters.n: Once again Noah obeys fully. His steady obedience is the heart of his story.
Noah is six hundred years old when the Flood begins—an old man who still did the hard work God asked.
Noah’s family of eight enters the ark. Peter later notes that “eight souls were saved by water.”

f.g: Her name is not given in the Bible.

chapters.n: Every kind of creature—clean and unclean, birds and creeping things—is included. God’s care extends to all life.

f.g: Even animals not used for sacrifice were preserved; all creation matters to God.

chapters.n: The animals enter in pairs, just as God commanded.

f.g: In pairs; the more detailed sevens of clean animals are summarized here.

chapters.n: After seven days the floodwaters come. The waiting period ends exactly as God said.
The date is carefully recorded, like a ship’s log. Water bursts up from below and pours down from above, as if the waters God separated at creation crash together again.

f.w: the fountains of the great deep
f.g: Underground waters and the deep sea (compare Genesis 1:2).
A poetic picture of floodgates in the sky.

chapters.n: The rain falls for forty days and nights.
The narrator repeats who entered the ark, naming each family member. The repetition stresses that God kept every one safe.

f.g: On that very same day.

chapters.n: Every kind of animal and bird enters with them. The phrase “after his kind” echoes Genesis 1—the ark carries a whole creation into a new world.
All breathing creatures come in pairs to Noah.
A tender detail: the Lord Himself shuts the door. Noah’s safety rests in God’s hands, and the time for entering has ended.
The waters rise and lift the ark above the earth. What destroys the world also carries the faithful to safety.

f.g: Lifted and carried.

chapters.n: The waters “prevail”—they dominate—while the ark floats peacefully on top.

f.g: Grew strong; overpowered.

chapters.n: The waters cover even the high hills. Many Latter-day Saint leaders have compared the Flood to a baptism of the earth.
The water stands about 22 feet above the mountains, enough for the ark to float clear.

f.g: About 22 feet (7 meters)—roughly half the ark’s height, which may be how the depth was gauged.

chapters.n: All life on land dies—every bird, animal, creeping thing, and person outside the ark.
The narrator emphasizes that everything that breathed on dry land died. Creatures in the sea are not mentioned.

f.g: Echoes Genesis 2:7—the gift of life is withdrawn.

chapters.n: Everything is wiped away; only Noah and those with him remain. A small faithful remnant carries God’s purposes forward—a pattern repeated throughout scripture.
The waters dominate the earth for 150 days—about five months. The faithful must wait patiently inside the ark.

This is the turning point of the Flood story: “God remembered Noah.” In scripture, God’s remembering means He acts on His promises. A wind blows over the waters, echoing the Spirit moving over the waters at creation.

f.g: To “remember” in Hebrew means to act faithfully for someone, not just to recall.
Hebrew ruaḥ — wind, breath, or spirit; the same word as in Genesis 1:2.
Subsided; went down.

chapters.n: The sources of the flood are shut off above and below. The chaos is brought back under God’s control.

f.g: Held back.

chapters.n: Slowly the waters recede. After 150 days they have noticeably gone down.

f.g: Decreased; lessened.

chapters.n: The ark comes to rest in the mountains of Ararat, a region in modern eastern Turkey and Armenia. The word “rested” echoes Noah’s name, which means rest.

f.g: The ancient land of Urartu, around eastern Turkey and Armenia—a region, not necessarily the single peak known today as Mount Ararat.
Hebrew nuaḥ, the root of Noah’s name.

chapters.n: Months pass before mountaintops appear. Noah’s faith requires long patience.

f.g: About two and a half months after the ark grounded.

chapters.n: After forty more days Noah opens the window. He is cautious and patient, testing before acting.
Noah sends a raven, which flies back and forth. Ravens eat carrion and can survive outside, so it does not return with useful news.

f.g: Back and forth.

chapters.n: Next Noah sends a dove—a gentle bird that needs dry land and plants. Doves become a symbol of peace and of the Holy Ghost.
The dove finds nowhere to land and returns. Noah tenderly reaches out and draws her back into the ark—a small picture of God gathering in the weary.

f.w: no rest for the sole of her foot

chapters.n: Noah waits seven more days, then sends the dove again. Hope and patience go together.

f.g: Waited.

chapters.n: The dove returns with a freshly plucked olive leaf—proof that trees are growing again. The olive leaf has become a lasting symbol of peace and new life.

f.g: Joseph Smith called D&C 88 “the olive leaf … plucked from the Tree of Paradise, the Lord’s message of peace to us.”
Freshly picked—not floating debris.

chapters.n: After another week, the dove does not return; she has found a home. The earth is ready for life again.

f.w: returned not again unto him any more
f.g: The dove’s absence is good news.

chapters.n: On New Year’s Day of Noah’s 601st year, the ground is dry. Noah removes the covering and sees a new world. A new year, a new beginning.

f.w: the first month, the first day of the month
f.g: The earth’s renewal falls on a New Year’s Day.
The roof or cover of the ark.

chapters.n: Almost two months later the earth is fully dry. Noah and his family had been in the ark about a year in all.

f.g: Counting from 7:11, about a year and ten days.

chapters.n: Noah waited for God’s word before leaving the ark, just as he had waited before entering it. God now speaks.

f.g: Noah did not leave on his own judgment, even though the ground was dry.

chapters.n: God tells the whole family to go out. As at entering, so at leaving: they move at God’s command.
The animals are to go out and multiply. God renews the creation blessing of Genesis 1—this is a fresh start for the earth.
Noah and his family step out into the cleansed earth.

f.g: Noah again obeys immediately.

chapters.n: Every creature leaves by families, in order, after their kinds.

f.g: Literally “by their families”—an orderly exodus.

chapters.n: Noah’s first act is worship. He builds an altar—the first one named in the Bible—and offers sacrifices of clean animals in gratitude. Sacrifice pointed forward to Jesus Christ.

f.g: Offerings wholly burned on the altar, symbolizing total dedication to God.

chapters.n: The Lord accepts the offering and resolves never again to curse the ground or destroy all life this way, though human hearts are still prone to evil. God’s mercy, not human goodness, guarantees the future.

f.g: A pleasing aroma—a way of saying God accepted the offering.

chapters.n: God promises that the seasons and the cycle of day and night will continue as long as the earth lasts. Every sunrise and harvest is a reminder of His faithfulness.
God renews the very first blessing of Genesis 1 to Noah’s family. Noah becomes like a second Adam, the father of a renewed human race.

f.w: Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth

chapters.n: The relationship between people and animals changes. Animals will now fear humans, and humans are given authority over them—a stewardship that carries responsibility.

f.w: the fear of you and the dread of you
f.g: A new reality after the Flood: animals will be wary of people.

chapters.n: For the first time God explicitly permits people to eat animal flesh, just as He had earlier given plants. Latter-day revelation adds that meat is to be used sparingly and with thanksgiving.

f.g: Food.

f.w: Every moving thing that liveth shall be meat for you

chapters.n: One limit: they must not eat meat with its blood. Blood represents life, which belongs to God. This principle runs through the law of Moses and points to the sacred blood of Christ.

f.w: the life thereof, which is the blood thereof

chapters.n: God will hold every creature and person accountable for taking a human life. The JST adds that animals’ blood must not be shed wastefully either.

f.g: Will demand an accounting for. JST Genesis 9:10-11 adds that blood should not be shed except for food to save life, and warns against wasting flesh.

chapters.n: Murder is the gravest offense because every person bears God’s image. The verse is crafted as a poetic mirror: shed—blood—man / man—blood—shed.

f.w: in the image of God made he man

chapters.n: God repeats His command to have children and fill the earth. The renewed world is meant to teem with life again.

f.g: Literally “swarm,” as living things did at creation (1:20).

chapters.n: God now speaks to Noah and all his sons together, introducing His covenant.

f.g: The covenant includes all of Noah’s descendants—all humanity.

chapters.n: God Himself makes the covenant. It is His initiative and His promise, extending to future generations.
Remarkably, the covenant also includes every animal. God’s promises reach to all living things.
The promise: never again will a flood destroy all life on the earth. Latter-day scripture teaches that the earth’s future cleansing will be by fire, not water.

f.w: neither shall there any more be a flood

chapters.n: God gives a visible sign of His covenant, one that will last through all generations.

f.g: A sign or reminder of the covenant.

chapters.n: God places the rainbow in the clouds as the sign. The Hebrew word for bow also means a warrior’s bow—some see God hanging up His weapon in peace.

f.g: Hebrew qeshet — a rainbow, but also an archer’s bow.

chapters.n: Whenever storm clouds gather, the rainbow will appear as a comforting sign.

f.w: the bow shall be seen in the cloud

chapters.n: God says He will remember His covenant. The rainbow reminds God as well as people—an image of His faithfulness.
The JST adds that when God looks on the bow He will remember the covenant made with Enoch: that in the last days Zion would return and the earth would rejoice.

f.g: JST Genesis 9:21-25 links the rainbow to God’s covenant with Enoch that Zion would return.

chapters.n: God repeats that the rainbow is the sign of His covenant with all life—three times in a few verses, for emphasis.

f.w: This is the token of the covenant
f.g: The repetition seals the promise.

chapters.n: Noah’s three sons are named, with a note that Ham is the father of Canaan—setting up the next story and later Israel’s relationship with the Canaanites.

f.g: Ancestor of the Canaanites, who lived in the land later promised to Abraham.

chapters.n: All the earth’s peoples descend from these three sons. The next chapter traces their families in detail.

f.g: Scattered and populated.

chapters.n: Noah becomes a farmer and plants a vineyard—the first vineyard mentioned in scripture.

f.g: A farmer; one who works the soil.

chapters.n: Noah drinks too much wine and lies exposed in his tent. Scripture honestly records the failings of even great prophets.

f.g: Some Latter-day Saint readers note that the JST does not remove this event.
Exposed; lying uncovered.

chapters.n: Ham sees his father’s shame and tells his brothers, apparently making a mockery of it rather than protecting his father’s dignity.

f.w: saw the nakedness of his father
f.g: The exact nature of Ham’s wrong is debated; at minimum it was disrespect and exposing his father’s shame.

chapters.n: Shem and Japheth respectfully cover their father, walking backward so as not to look. Their actions model honoring parents and protecting others’ dignity.
Noah wakes and learns what Ham had done.

f.g: Possibly “youngest”; Ham is usually listed second, so the phrase may mean “lesser” or refer to Canaan.

chapters.n: Noah curses Canaan, Ham’s son, to be a servant. Historically this foreshadows Israel’s later dominance over the Canaanites. The Church has firmly disavowed past ideas that used this curse to justify racism.

f.g: The curse is on Canaan specifically, not on all Ham’s descendants or any race.
A Hebrew way of saying “the lowest of servants.”

chapters.n: Noah blesses the God of Shem. Through Shem will come Abraham, Israel, and ultimately Jesus Christ.
Japheth will be enlarged—his name sounds like “enlarge”—and will dwell in Shem’s tents, sharing in Shem’s blessings. Many see a hint that other nations would one day share Israel’s covenant.

f.g: Wordplay: Japheth (yefet) and “enlarge” (yaft).

f.w: dwell in the tents of Shem

chapters.n: Noah lives 350 years after the Flood—long enough, by the Bible’s numbers, to overlap with Abraham’s early life.

f.g: By Genesis chronology Noah died about two years before Abraham’s birth, or later by some reckonings.

chapters.n: Noah dies at 950. With his death, the line of the pre-Flood patriarchs closes. Latter-day revelation teaches that Noah stands next to Adam in priesthood authority.
This chapter, often called the Table of Nations, maps how Noah’s descendants spread into peoples around the ancient world. It shows that every nation shares one family origin.

f.g: Hebrew toledot — family history; a section marker in Genesis.

chapters.n: Japheth’s sons are listed first. Many of these names match peoples north and west of Israel, such as the Medes (Madai) and Greeks (Javan).

f.g: The Ionians or Greeks.
The Medes of ancient Iran.

chapters.n: Gomer’s descendants probably settled around the Black Sea and Asia Minor (modern Turkey).

f.g: Probably a people of eastern Asia Minor (compare Ezekiel 27:14).
A northern people; later Jewish tradition used the name for Germany.

chapters.n: Javan’s descendants are seafaring peoples of the Mediterranean, including Cyprus (Kittim) and perhaps Spain (Tarshish).

f.g: A distant port, possibly in Spain; Jonah later tried to flee there (Jonah 1:3).
Cyprus, and later used for western peoples generally.

chapters.n: These coastland peoples spread out, each with its own language and land. The phrase “after his tongue” anticipates the scattering of languages at Babel in chapter 11.

f.g: Coastlands and islands, especially around the Mediterranean.
Here simply “nations.”

chapters.n: Ham’s sons are linked with lands to the south and in Canaan: Cush (Nubia), Mizraim (Egypt), Phut (probably Libya), and Canaan.

f.g: The Hebrew name for Egypt.
The region south of Egypt (Nubia/Sudan).

chapters.n: Cush’s descendants are linked with Arabia and East Africa, such as Sheba, famous later for its queen who visited Solomon.

f.g: A trading people of northwestern Arabia.

chapters.n: Nimrod is introduced as the first great “mighty one”—a warrior and empire-builder.

f.g: A powerful warrior or tyrant; the same word (gibbor) used of the men of renown in 6:4.

chapters.n: Nimrod becomes proverbial as a mighty hunter. “Before the LORD” may mean “in God’s sight” or even “in defiance of God”; later Jewish tradition remembered him as rebellious.

f.g: Can mean “in the sight of” or “against” the Lord.

chapters.n: Nimrod’s kingdom begins in famous Mesopotamian cities like Babel (Babylon), Erech (Uruk), and Accad. This sets the stage for the tower of Babel in chapter 11.

f.g: Babylon, which becomes a symbol of worldly pride throughout scripture.
Southern Mesopotamia (modern Iraq).

chapters.n: From there, power extends north into Assyria and its great cities, including Nineveh. Assyria later conquers the northern kingdom of Israel.

f.g: Assyria; the phrase may also mean Nimrod “went out into Assyria.”

chapters.n: Resen lies between Nineveh and Calah, together forming a great urban region.

f.g: Later known as Nimrud, a major Assyrian capital.

chapters.n: Egypt’s descendants are listed by peoples, most of whom are now hard to identify.

f.g: Probably a North African people.

chapters.n: Among Egypt’s offshoots are the Philistines, Israel’s later rivals, connected here with Caphtor, probably Crete.

f.g: The Philistines.
People of Caphtor, likely Crete.

chapters.n: Canaan’s sons include Sidon, a major Phoenician city, and Heth, ancestor of the Hittites. Abraham will later buy a burial place from the sons of Heth.

f.g: A major Phoenician port city on the coast of modern Lebanon.

chapters.n: These are peoples Israel will encounter in the promised land, such as the Jebusites of Jerusalem and the Amorites.

f.g: The inhabitants of Jerusalem before David captured it.

chapters.n: More Canaanite peoples are named, some linked with cities on the coast of Syria and Lebanon.
The Canaanite families spread through the land.

f.g: People of Hamath, a city in Syria.

chapters.n: The borders of Canaan are traced from Sidon to Gaza and to the cities near the Dead Sea, including Sodom and Gomorrah. This is the land later promised to Abraham.

f.g: Location unknown, probably near the Dead Sea.

chapters.n: A summary closes Ham’s line: families, languages, lands, and nations.

f.g: By their languages.

chapters.n: Shem is introduced as the ancestor of “all the children of Eber.” From Eber’s name comes the word “Hebrew,” so Shem’s line leads to Abraham and Israel.

f.g: Likely the source of the word “Hebrew.”

f.w: the brother of Japheth the elder
f.g: Can mean either Shem or Japheth was the elder; the Hebrew is ambiguous.

chapters.n: Shem’s sons include peoples to the east and north: Elam (in Iran), Asshur (Assyria), and Aram (Syria). Arphaxad leads to Abraham.

f.g: The Arameans of Syria; Abraham’s relatives later live there (Genesis 24:10).

chapters.n: Aram’s sons include Uz, a name also given to Job’s homeland.
The line runs from Arphaxad to Salah to Eber, the ancestor of the Hebrews.
In Peleg’s day “the earth was divided.” Peleg means “division.” This may refer to the scattering at Babel; some Latter-day Saints have also connected it with a division of land masses.

f.g: Means “division.”

chapters.n: Joktan’s sons are listed. Many seem to be tribes of the Arabian Peninsula, such as Hazarmaveth (Hadramaut in Yemen).

f.g: Likely the Hadramaut region of southern Arabia.

chapters.n: More of Joktan’s descendants, likely Arabian tribes.

f.g: Possibly an old name for Sanaa in Yemen.

chapters.n: Joktan’s line also includes another Sheba, showing the name was shared by more than one people.

f.g: A southern Arabian kingdom; compare the Cushite Sheba in verse 7.

chapters.n: Ophir becomes famous for fine gold in Solomon’s day.
Joktan’s families settle across a region “of the east,” likely in Arabia.

f.g: Eastern hill country; exact locations are uncertain.

chapters.n: A summary closes Shem’s line.

f.g: Organized by family, language, land, and nation.

chapters.n: The chapter ends by stating that all nations came from Noah’s sons. The Bible’s story is ultimately about one human family, which God will bless through Abraham.

f.w: by these were the nations divided

chapters.n: After the Flood, all people share one language. This story explains how the many languages and nations of chapter 10 came about.

f.g: Literally “one lip and the same words.”

chapters.n: Migrating people settle on a plain in Shinar, the region of Babylon in southern Mesopotamia.

f.g: Or “eastward”; in Genesis, moving east often hints at moving away from God.

chapters.n: Lacking stone, they bake mud bricks and use tar as mortar—real building methods of ancient Mesopotamia. The narrator gently contrasts their human-made materials with God’s creation.

f.g: An old expression meaning “Come on!” or “Let’s go!”
Bitumen or tar.
Thoroughly.

chapters.n: They plan a city and a towering structure to reach heaven and make a name for themselves. Their aim is human glory and security without God—exactly the opposite of God’s command to fill the earth.

f.g: Likely a ziggurat, a stepped temple-tower common in Mesopotamia.

f.w: let us make us a name

chapters.n: With gentle irony, the narrator says the Lord had to “come down” to see the tower that was supposed to reach heaven. Their greatest effort is tiny to God.

f.g: A picture of God investigating before judging (compare Genesis 18:21).

chapters.n: God observes that a united humanity bent on pride will stop at nothing. Unity is good, but unity in rebellion only multiplies evil.

f.w: nothing will be restrained from them
f.g: Nothing will be impossible or held back for them.

chapters.n: God speaks again in the plural, “let us,” and confuses their language. Their own “let us” plans are answered by God’s “let us.”

f.g: To mix up or confuse.

chapters.n: God scatters them, and construction stops. What they feared—being scattered—happens anyway. The Book of Mormon tells of the Jaredites, who came from the tower and were led by God to the Americas.
The place is called Babel, which sounds like the Hebrew word for “confuse.” Babylon claimed its name meant “gate of God,” but Genesis turns the name into “confusion.”

f.g: Wordplay with Hebrew balal, “to confuse.” Babylonians understood Bab-ili as “gate of god.”

chapters.n: The story narrows from all nations to one family line, Shem’s, which leads to Abram. God’s plan to bless all nations will come through one family.

f.w: These are the generations of Shem

chapters.n: Shem lives five hundred more years. By the Bible’s numbers he would have lived into Abram’s lifetime.

f.g: Lifespans begin decreasing noticeably after the Flood.

chapters.n: Arphaxad fathers Salah. Notice how the ages at which men become fathers are now much younger than before the Flood.
Arphaxad lives 403 more years.

f.g: Years Arphaxad lived after Salah’s birth.

chapters.n: Salah fathers Eber, the ancestor of the Hebrews.
Salah lives 403 more years.

f.g: Years Salah lived after Eber’s birth.

chapters.n: Eber fathers Peleg, in whose days the earth was divided.
Eber lives 430 more years.

f.g: Eber’s total life of 464 years is the longest after Shem’s in this list.

chapters.n: Peleg fathers Reu. From Peleg on, lifespans drop sharply.

f.g: Means perhaps “friend.”

chapters.n: Peleg lives 209 more years—his total of 239 is about half that of his father.

f.g: Years Peleg lived after Reu’s birth.

chapters.n: Reu fathers Serug.

f.g: Also the name of a town near Haran in northern Mesopotamia.

chapters.n: Reu lives 207 more years.

f.g: Years Reu lived after Serug’s birth.

chapters.n: Serug fathers Nahor, Abram’s grandfather.

f.g: Abram will also have a brother named Nahor (verse 26).

chapters.n: Serug lives two hundred more years.

f.g: Years Serug lived after Nahor’s birth.

chapters.n: Nahor fathers Terah, Abram’s father.
Nahor lives 119 more years.

f.g: Nahor’s total of 148 years is the shortest in this list.

chapters.n: Terah becomes father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran. With Abram, the story of God’s covenant people truly begins.

f.g: Means “exalted father”; later renamed Abraham (17:5).

chapters.n: Terah’s family record is introduced, including Lot, Abram’s nephew, who will play an important role in coming chapters.
Haran dies in Ur, his hometown. The book of Abraham says Ur was full of idolatry, and that a famine struck the land.

f.g: Usually identified with Ur in southern Iraq, though some propose a northern location.

chapters.n: Abram marries Sarai, and Nahor marries his niece Milcah. These family ties will matter later, when Isaac and Jacob find wives among Nahor’s descendants.

f.g: Possibly “princess”; later renamed Sarah (17:15).

chapters.n: A brief, heartbreaking note: Sarai cannot have children. This sets up the central tension of Abram’s story—how can God’s promise of countless descendants come true?

f.g: Unable to have children.

chapters.n: Terah leads the family out of Ur toward Canaan, but they stop and settle in Haran. The book of Abraham clarifies that the Lord called Abraham to leave Ur, and Terah followed.

f.w: they went forth with them from Ur of the Chaldees

f.g: A trading city in northern Mesopotamia (modern Turkey), not the same as Abram’s brother Haran.

chapters.n: Terah dies in Haran at 205. The book of Abraham records that Terah returned to his idolatry there.

God calls Abram to leave everything familiar—homeland, relatives, and father’s household—and go to a land God will reveal. Abram’s journey of faith begins with trusting God without knowing exactly where he is going.

f.w: Get thee out of thy country

f.g: Show.

chapters.n: God promises Abram a great nation, blessing, and a great name. Unlike the builders of Babel, who tried to make a name for themselves, Abram receives a name as God’s gift—and he is to be a blessing to others.

This is the heart of the Abrahamic covenant: through Abram all the world’s families will be blessed. The book of Abraham explains this includes the gospel, the priesthood, and eternal life for all who receive it.

f.w: in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed

chapters.n: Abram obeys and leaves Haran with his nephew Lot. Genesis gives his age as seventy-five; the book of Abraham says sixty-two, perhaps counting a different departure.

f.w: So Abram departed, as the LORD had spoken unto him

f.g: Abraham 2:14 says Abraham was sixty-two when he left Haran.

chapters.n: Abram brings his family, wealth, and “the souls that they had gotten in Haran.” The book of Abraham explains these were people they had converted to the Lord.

f.w: the souls that they had gotten in Haran

f.g: Possessions; wealth.

chapters.n: Abram reaches Shechem, at the great tree of Moreh in the heart of Canaan. The land is already occupied by Canaanites—the promise will take faith and time.

f.g: Shechem, a town in the central hill country between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim.
Better “the oak (or terebinth) of Moreh,” perhaps a well-known sacred tree. Moreh means “teacher.”

chapters.n: The Lord appears and promises this very land to Abram’s descendants. Abram responds by building an altar—worship marks his path through the land.

f.w: Unto thy seed will I give this land

chapters.n: Abram moves to the hills between Bethel and Ai, builds another altar, and calls on the Lord’s name. His life becomes a trail of altars and prayers.

f.g: Means “house of God”; it receives this name later from Jacob (28:19).
Ai, a town east of Bethel (Joshua 7:2).

f.w: called upon the name of the LORD

chapters.n: Abram keeps moving south toward the Negev, the dry region of southern Canaan.

f.g: Toward the Negev, the arid southern land.

chapters.n: A severe famine strikes, and Abram goes down to Egypt, whose Nile River made its crops more reliable. Famine drives several patriarchs to Egypt, a pattern that will shape Israel’s story.

f.g: To live somewhere temporarily as a foreigner.

chapters.n: Abram realizes that Sarai’s beauty could endanger them. Though she was about sixty-five, people then lived longer, and she was still striking.

f.w: a fair woman to look upon

chapters.n: Abram fears that the Egyptians will kill him to take Sarai.

f.g: In the ancient world, a powerful ruler might eliminate a husband to claim his wife.

chapters.n: Abram asks Sarai to say she is his sister. The book of Abraham records that the Lord instructed Abraham to do this. Sarai was in fact his half-sister (20:12).
As expected, the Egyptians notice Sarai’s beauty.

f.g: Saw; looked at.

chapters.n: Pharaoh’s officials praise Sarai to the king, and she is taken into his household, presumably to become a wife.

f.g: The title of Egypt’s king, meaning “great house.”
Praised.

chapters.n: Pharaoh treats Abram well and gives him livestock and servants. The gifts suggest Pharaoh considered them a bride-price.

f.g: Treated.
Male donkeys.

chapters.n: The Lord protects Sarai by striking Pharaoh’s household with plagues. God guards the mother of the promised line—foreshadowing the later plagues on Egypt in Moses’ day.

f.g: Struck with afflictions or diseases.

chapters.n: Pharaoh confronts Abram, sensing that the plagues came because Sarai was married.

f.w: What is this that thou hast done unto me?
f.g: The same kind of question God asked Eve (3:13).

chapters.n: Pharaoh returns Sarai and tells them to leave. The foreign king behaves honorably once he knows the truth.

f.w: take her, and go thy way

chapters.n: Pharaoh sends Abram away with all he had. Like Israel later, Abram leaves Egypt richer than he arrived.
Abram leaves Egypt with his family and Lot and returns to the Negev in southern Canaan.

f.g: Travelers “go up” to Canaan’s higher ground and “go down” to Egypt.
The Negev.

chapters.n: Abram is now wealthy. In that culture, livestock and precious metals were the main forms of wealth. His riches will soon test his relationship with Lot.

f.g: Literally “very heavy”—weighed down with wealth.

chapters.n: Abram retraces his steps back to Bethel, where he had camped before going to Egypt. Returning to the place of the altar suggests spiritual renewal.
At the old altar Abram worships again, calling on the Lord’s name. After the troubles in Egypt, he comes back to where he first met God in the land.

f.w: called on the name of the LORD

chapters.n: Lot too has grown wealthy, with his own flocks, herds, and tents—he prospered by traveling with Abram.

f.g: Representing households and servants, not just shelters.

chapters.n: The land cannot support both of their large herds. Prosperity brings its own problems.

f.g: Support; sustain.

chapters.n: Their herdsmen quarrel over water and grazing land. The mention of Canaanites and Perizzites reminds us they were outsiders in a land already occupied—disunity was dangerous.

f.g: Conflict; quarreling.
A people of the Canaanite hill country; the name may mean “village-dwellers.”

chapters.n: Abram, the elder, takes the lead in making peace. Family relationships matter more to him than winning an argument.

f.g: “Brethren” here means close relatives.

chapters.n: With great generosity, Abram lets Lot choose first. He trusts God to provide, whatever Lot picks.

f.g: Directions were often given facing east: left meant north, right meant south.

chapters.n: Lot looks out and sees the lush Jordan valley, as green as Eden or Egypt. The narrator’s aside—“before the LORD destroyed Sodom”—warns that looks can deceive.

f.g: The circle or valley of the Jordan near the Dead Sea.

chapters.n: Lot chooses the best-looking land and moves east. Once again, moving “east” in Genesis signals drifting from God’s presence.
Abram stays in Canaan, the land of promise, while Lot settles among the cities of the plain and moves his tent ever closer to Sodom.

f.g: Lot moves step by step toward Sodom; by 14:12 and 19:1 he lives inside the city.

chapters.n: The narrator bluntly warns that Sodom’s people were extremely wicked. Lot chose by appearances without weighing spiritual danger.

f.w: the men of Sodom were wicked

chapters.n: After Lot leaves, God speaks to Abram and tells him to look in every direction. Lot looked with his own eyes and chose; now God invites Abram to look and receive.

f.g: Echoes verse 10, where Lot “lifted up his eyes.”

chapters.n: God promises all the land Abram can see to him and his descendants forever. Abram’s generosity loses him nothing.
God also promises descendants as countless as the dust of the earth—an astonishing promise to a man with no children.

f.w: as the dust of the earth

chapters.n: God invites Abram to walk the land’s length and breadth, as an owner surveys property. Walking the land was a way of claiming it.

f.g: In the ancient world, walking over land could symbolize taking possession of it.

chapters.n: Abram settles by the great trees of Mamre near Hebron and builds another altar. Hebron becomes his main home and later the family burial place.

f.g: Better “the oaks (or terebinths) of Mamre,” named after an Amorite ally (14:13).

chapters.n: The story widens to international politics. Four kings from Mesopotamia and beyond form an alliance. Their identities in history are uncertain, but the names fit the region and era.

f.g: Babylonia (compare 10:10; 11:2).
A kingdom in southwestern Iran.
Hebrew goyim, perhaps a coalition of peoples.

chapters.n: These eastern kings attack five city-kings near the Dead Sea, including the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah.
The five kings gather in the valley of Siddim, an area later covered by or bordering the Dead Sea, called here the “salt sea.”

f.g: The Dead Sea, so salty that almost nothing can live in it.

chapters.n: The five cities had been subject to Chedorlaomer for twelve years and then rebelled, refusing to pay tribute.

f.g: Paid tribute as subject states.

chapters.n: Chedorlaomer’s coalition sweeps down the east side of the Jordan, defeating several peoples remembered as giants or ancient inhabitants.

f.g: An ancient people remembered as giants (Deuteronomy 2:10-11, 20-21).
Another early people of the region east of the Dead Sea (Deuteronomy 2:10).

chapters.n: They push on into the mountains of Seir (later Edom) as far as the edge of the wilderness.

f.g: Early inhabitants of Seir, later displaced by Esau’s descendants (Deuteronomy 2:12).
Probably near Elath on the Gulf of Aqaba.

chapters.n: Turning back north, they strike Kadesh and the lands of the Amalekites and Amorites. The campaign forms a great loop around the Dead Sea region.

f.g: An oasis in the northern Sinai; Israel later camps there (Numbers 20:1).
“Spring of judgment.”

chapters.n: The five rebel kings come out to fight the invaders in the valley of Siddim.

f.g: Engaged in battle.

chapters.n: Four kings against five—the larger number loses, showing how powerful the eastern alliance was.

f.g: A neat summary of the conflict.

chapters.n: The valley is full of tar pits. The fleeing kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fall into them or hide there; the rest escape to the hills.

f.g: Bitumen or tar pits—natural asphalt deposits common around the Dead Sea.

chapters.n: The invaders plunder Sodom and Gomorrah of goods and food supplies.

f.g: Food and provisions.

chapters.n: Lot, who now lives in Sodom itself, is captured with his possessions. His choice to live near and then in Sodom has put him in danger.
A survivor brings the news to “Abram the Hebrew,” who is living among friendly Amorite allies near Hebron. This is the first time the word “Hebrew” appears in the Bible.

f.g: First use of “Hebrew,” perhaps from Eber (10:21) or meaning “one from across” the river.
Allied by treaty.

chapters.n: Abram immediately rescues his nephew, gathering 318 trained men from his own household and chasing the invaders far to the north.

f.g: Here “brother” means close relative—Lot is his nephew.
The northern town later named Dan (Judges 18:29); the narrator uses the familiar later name.

chapters.n: Abram divides his forces and attacks by night, a clever strategy that routs the larger army and pursues them past Damascus.

f.g: A place north of Damascus; location uncertain.
North of (when facing east).

chapters.n: Abram recovers everything—Lot, his goods, the women, and the other captives. Abram blesses others, just as God promised he would.

f.g: Brought back; restored.

chapters.n: The king of Sodom comes out to meet the victorious Abram in the King’s Valley, likely near Jerusalem.

f.g: The King’s Valley, probably near Jerusalem (compare 2 Samuel 18:18).

chapters.n: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of the Most High God, brings bread and wine. Latter-day scripture greatly honors him as a great high priest, after whom the higher priesthood is named.

f.g: Means “king of righteousness.”
Means “peace”; traditionally identified with Jerusalem (Psalms 76:2).
Many see a foreshadowing of the sacrament. JST Genesis 14:25-40 greatly expands Melchizedek’s story.

chapters.n: Melchizedek blesses Abram in the name of God, owner of heaven and earth. Doctrine and Covenants teaches that Abraham received the priesthood from Melchizedek.

f.g: Creator or owner.

chapters.n: Melchizedek praises God for the victory, and Abram gives him a tenth of everything. This is the first mention of tithing in the Bible.

f.g: A tenth.

chapters.n: The king of Sodom offers Abram the captured goods if he will return the people. His offer contrasts sharply with Melchizedek’s gift.

f.g: He wants his subjects back; he offers Abram the plunder.

chapters.n: Abram says he has sworn an oath to the Most High God, using the same title Melchizedek used. He identifies the LORD with Melchizedek’s God.

f.w: I have lift up mine hand
f.g: Raising the hand was a gesture of taking an oath.

chapters.n: Abram refuses even a thread or sandal strap from Sodom. He wants no one but God to get credit for his prosperity.

f.g: A sandal strap.

f.w: lest thou shouldest say, I have made Abram rich

chapters.n: Abram asks only for what his men ate and for his allies’ fair share. He holds himself to a high standard but is fair to others.

After the battle and his refusal of Sodom’s riches, Abram may have feared revenge or wondered about his reward. God comforts him in a vision: God Himself is Abram’s protection and his greatest reward.

f.g: The first “fear not” in the Bible, a phrase God often uses to comfort His servants.
Hebrew maḥazeh — something seen by revelation.

chapters.n: Abram honestly pours out his concern: what good are rewards if he has no child? His servant Eliezer of Damascus stands to inherit everything.

f.g: Hebrew ’Adonai YHWH—“my Lord, Jehovah.”
Household manager.

chapters.n: Abram repeats his worry. Ancient custom allowed a childless man to adopt a trusted servant as heir. Abram is not rebellious, just honest with God about his pain.

f.g: A servant born into his household.

chapters.n: God answers clearly: Abram’s heir will be his own son, not a servant.

f.g: From your own body—your biological child.

chapters.n: God takes Abram outside and shows him the night sky: “count the stars—so shall your descendants be.” The book of Abraham also records the Lord showing Abraham the stars and promising innumerable posterity.

f.g: “Tell” means count.

chapters.n: Abram believes God, and God counts his faith as righteousness. Paul uses this verse as a key example of faith in God’s promises.

f.g: Credited or reckoned to his account.

chapters.n: God reminds Abram that He brought him out of Ur in order to give him this land. The book of Abraham tells how the Lord rescued him from idolatrous priests there.

f.w: brought thee out of Ur of the Chaldees

chapters.n: Abram asks how he can know he will inherit the land. The JST adds that Abram saw the days of the Son of Man and rejoiced, learning that the promise looked forward to resurrection.

f.g: JST Genesis 15:9-12 adds that Abram saw the days of the Son of Man and believed.

chapters.n: God commands Abram to prepare animals for a covenant ceremony. These are the same kinds of animals later used in Israel’s sacrifices.

f.g: A young cow.
A small dove.

chapters.n: Abram cuts the animals in half and lays the halves opposite each other. In ancient covenants, parties would walk between the pieces, saying in effect, “May this happen to me if I break my word.”
Birds of prey swoop down on the carcasses, and Abram drives them away. Faith sometimes means guarding sacred things while waiting on God.

f.g: Birds of prey, such as vultures.

chapters.n: As the sun sets, Abram falls into a deep sleep, and a terrifying darkness comes over him—a sign of the hard times his descendants will face.

f.g: The same word used of Adam’s sleep in 2:21—a state for divine action and revelation.

chapters.n: God reveals that Abram’s descendants will be foreigners and slaves in another land for four hundred years. This foreshadows Israel’s bondage in Egypt.
God promises to judge the oppressing nation, and Israel will leave with great wealth—fulfilled in the Exodus.
Abram himself will die peacefully at a good old age. God’s promises are often fulfilled beyond a single lifetime.

f.g: An idiom for dying and joining one’s ancestors.

chapters.n: The delay is partly because the Amorites’ wickedness has not yet reached its full measure. God is patient even with the wicked, giving them time to repent before judgment.

f.w: the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full

f.g: Probably long generations of about a century each.

chapters.n: In the darkness, a smoking firepot and a blazing torch pass between the pieces—representing God Himself. Only God walks through, showing He alone guarantees this covenant.

f.w: a smoking furnace, and a burning lamp
f.g: Fire and smoke often signal God’s presence, as in the pillar of fire and Sinai.

chapters.n: God formally “cuts” a covenant, promising the land from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates. This territory was most nearly reached in the days of David and Solomon.

f.g: Literally “cut a covenant,” fitting the ceremony.
Probably the Wadi el-Arish on Egypt’s border, or the Nile.

chapters.n: The peoples then living in the land are listed, beginning with lesser-known groups.

f.g: A people later friendly to Israel; Moses’ father-in-law was a Kenite (Judges 1:16).

chapters.n: The list continues with the Hittites, Perizzites, and Rephaim.
The list closes with the main peoples of Canaan, including the Jebusites of Jerusalem. Ten nations are named in all—a number suggesting completeness.
Ten years have passed, and Sarai still has no children. Her Egyptian servant, Hagar, is introduced—perhaps acquired during their stay in Egypt (12:16).

f.g: A female servant, usually personally attached to her mistress.

chapters.n: Sarai proposes a custom known from ancient Near Eastern documents: a childless wife could give her servant to her husband, and the child would count as hers. Abram agrees.

f.w: I may obtain children by her
f.g: Literally “I may be built up by her”—Hebrew banah (build) sounds like ben (son).

f.w: Abram hearkened to the voice of Sarai

chapters.n: Sarai gives Hagar to Abram as a wife. Latter-day revelation teaches that Sarah did this in keeping with God’s law, and that Abraham was not condemned for it.
Hagar becomes pregnant and begins to look down on Sarai. In a culture that prized children, motherhood raised Hagar’s status and hurt Sarai deeply.

f.g: Looked on with contempt; treated as lesser.

chapters.n: Sarai blames Abram for the tension and calls on the Lord to judge. Plans made to help often bring unexpected heartache.

f.g: “You are responsible for the wrong done to me.”

chapters.n: Abram leaves the matter to Sarai, who treats Hagar harshly, and Hagar runs away. Scripture does not hide the flaws of its heroes.

f.g: Treated her harshly. The same Hebrew word describes Egypt’s oppression of Israel (Exodus 1:11-12).

chapters.n: The angel of the Lord finds Hagar by a spring on the road back toward Egypt. God seeks out the outsider, the servant, the runaway.

f.g: A heavenly messenger who speaks with God’s own voice; this is his first appearance in the Bible.
A desert region between Canaan and Egypt.

chapters.n: The angel calls Hagar by name and asks where she has come from and where she is going—questions that invite reflection, much like God’s questions in Eden.

f.w: whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go?
f.g: “Where have you come from, and where are you going?”

chapters.n: The angel tells Hagar to return and submit to Sarai. It is a hard instruction, but it comes with promises of blessing.

f.g: Humble yourself.

chapters.n: Hagar receives a promise much like Abram’s: descendants too many to count. God’s care reaches beyond the covenant line.

f.w: I will multiply thy seed exceedingly

chapters.n: Hagar is told to name her son Ishmael, “God hears,” because the Lord has heard her suffering.

f.g: Means “God hears.”

f.w: the LORD hath heard thy affliction

chapters.n: Ishmael will live free and fierce, like a wild donkey in the desert, never subject to anyone. This describes the independent desert peoples descended from him.

f.g: Literally “a wild donkey of a man”—free-roaming and untamed, not a criticism of his character.

f.w: in the presence of all his brethren
f.g: Or “in defiance of” or “east of” his relatives.

chapters.n: Hagar gives God a name: “Thou God seest me.” She is the only person in the Bible to name God. The overlooked servant discovers that God sees her.

f.g: Hebrew El Roi—“the God who sees me.”

chapters.n: The spring is named “Well of the Living One who sees me,” a reminder of God’s care in the wilderness.

f.g: “Well of the Living One who sees me.” Isaac later lives near here (24:62; 25:11).

chapters.n: Hagar returns and gives birth, and Abram names his son Ishmael—confirming the name given by the angel.
Abram is eighty-six when Ishmael is born. Thirteen more years will pass before God speaks again about the promised son through Sarai.

f.g: Eighty-six (a “score” is twenty).

chapters.n: Thirteen years after Ishmael’s birth, the Lord appears to Abram, now ninety-nine. God reveals Himself as “the Almighty” and calls Abram to live faithfully in His presence and be whole-hearted.
