f.g: Hebrew El Shaddai, a name of God emphasizing His power and sufficiency.
Be whole, complete, blameless.

chapters.n: God promises to confirm His covenant and greatly multiply Abram’s family.
Abram falls on his face in reverence, a natural response to God’s holy presence.

f.g: Bowed to the ground in worship.

chapters.n: God declares that Abram will be the father of many nations. The covenant reaches far beyond one people.
God renames Abram to Abraham. A new name marks a new identity and covenant relationship—a pattern found in baptism, the temple, and taking Christ’s name upon us.

f.g: Abram means “exalted father”; Abraham is explained as “father of a multitude.”

chapters.n: Nations and kings will come from Abraham—fulfilled through Israel’s kings, including David, and ultimately the King of kings, Jesus Christ.

f.w: kings shall come out of thee

chapters.n: The heart of the covenant: God will be their God forever. Latter-day Saints understand this as the everlasting covenant of the gospel, renewed in our day.

f.w: to be a God unto thee

chapters.n: God promises the land of Canaan as an everlasting possession, though Abraham still lives there as a foreigner.

f.g: A resident foreigner without property rights.

chapters.n: Abraham and his descendants have their part: to keep the covenant. Covenants involve promises on both sides.
Circumcision is given as the sign of the covenant for every male. This physical mark would remind God’s people that they belonged to Him.

f.g: Removal of the foreskin; for Israel, the outward sign of covenant membership.

chapters.n: Circumcision is a “token,” a sign. The JST explains it was given partly because people had strayed from correct ordinances, including baptism.

f.g: JST Genesis 17:3-7 says people had departed from God’s ordinances and the baptism He commanded.

chapters.n: Boys are to be circumcised at eight days old, including servants born in the household or purchased. The JST connects the eighth day with the teaching that children become accountable at eight years.

f.g: JST Genesis 17:11-12 links this to children not being accountable until eight years old.

chapters.n: The covenant is to be “in your flesh,” a permanent reminder. Scripture later teaches that true circumcision is of the heart.

f.g: Must certainly.

f.w: my covenant shall be in your flesh

chapters.n: Refusing circumcision means breaking the covenant and being cut off from God’s people. To reject the sign is to reject the relationship.

f.g: Excluded from the covenant community.

chapters.n: Sarai also receives a new name: Sarah. She is fully part of the covenant, not just Abraham’s companion.

f.g: Both Sarai and Sarah are forms meaning “princess.”

chapters.n: God promises to bless Sarah personally and give her a son. She will be mother of nations and kings.
Abraham bows and laughs. His laughter may mix joy and disbelief at the thought of a 100-year-old father and 90-year-old mother. The name Isaac will come from this laughter.

f.g: Hebrew tsaḥaq, the root of Isaac’s name.

chapters.n: Abraham pleads for Ishmael, the son he already loves. It is a father’s prayer.

f.w: O that Ishmael might live before thee!
f.g: “May Ishmael live under your blessing!”

chapters.n: God insists: Sarah will bear a son, named Isaac, and the covenant will continue through him.

f.g: Means “he laughs.”

chapters.n: God answers Abraham’s prayer for Ishmael too. Ishmael will be blessed with many descendants and twelve princes—a great nation.

f.g: A wordplay on Ishmael’s name, “God hears.”

chapters.n: The covenant line, however, will run through Isaac, born to Sarah within a year.

f.w: at this set time in the next year

chapters.n: God finishes speaking and departs, “going up” from Abraham, suggesting a personal appearance.
That very day, Abraham obeys completely, circumcising every male in his household. His obedience is immediate.

f.g: On that very same day.

chapters.n: Abraham is ninety-nine when he is circumcised—an old man entering a new covenant sign.

f.g: Ninety-nine.

chapters.n: Ishmael is thirteen. Many Arab peoples later traditionally practiced circumcision around this age.

f.g: Ishmael too receives the covenant sign, though the covenant line will pass through Isaac.

chapters.n: Father and son are circumcised on the same day, sharing the covenant sign together.

f.g: Repeated to stress Abraham’s prompt obedience.

chapters.n: All the men of the household, including servants and foreigners, are circumcised. From the start, outsiders could join the covenant family.

f.w: bought with money of the stranger

chapters.n: The Lord appears to Abraham by the trees of Mamre as he sits at his tent door during the hottest part of the day, a time when travelers would normally rest.

f.g: Better “the oaks of Mamre,” near Hebron.

chapters.n: Abraham sees three men and runs—at ninety-nine, in the heat—to welcome them, bowing low. His eager hospitality is a model of kindness to strangers.

f.g: The JST describes them as holy men sent from God; one speaks for the Lord.

chapters.n: Abraham begs his guests to stay and let him serve them. He calls himself their servant—humility and hospitality go together.

f.g: The JST reads “My brethren.” The Hebrew can be a respectful “my lord” or the divine title.

chapters.n: He offers water to wash their dusty feet and shade to rest under—basic courtesies in a hot, dry land.
Abraham modestly offers “a morsel of bread,” then provides a feast. The visitors accept.

f.g: Refresh yourselves; strengthen your hearts with food.

chapters.n: Abraham hurries to Sarah, asking her to bake a large quantity of fresh bread from the finest flour.

f.g: About 20 quarts (22 liters) of flour—far more than three guests could eat; generous hospitality.
Round flatbreads baked on hot stones.

chapters.n: He runs to choose a tender calf for a servant to prepare. Meat was a rare luxury, reserved for honored guests.

f.g: Prepare; cook.

chapters.n: Abraham serves curds, milk, and meat, and stands nearby like a servant while they eat under the tree.

f.g: Probably curds or yogurt.

chapters.n: The visitors ask for Sarah by name—a surprising detail, since strangers would not know it. Their visit is about her.

f.g: Their knowledge of Sarah’s new name hints that they are no ordinary travelers.

chapters.n: The speaker promises to return the next year, when Sarah will have a son. Sarah, listening behind the tent door, overhears.

f.w: according to the time of life
f.g: “When the season comes around”—about this time next year.

chapters.n: The narrator explains that Sarah was long past childbearing age. Only a miracle could fulfill this promise.

f.g: Very advanced in years.

f.w: it ceased to be with Sarah after the manner of women
f.g: She had gone through menopause.

chapters.n: Sarah laughs to herself at the idea. Her laugh is understandable—she has waited decades, and now the promise sounds impossible.

f.g: Another wordplay on Isaac’s name, “he laughs.”
Grown old.

chapters.n: The Lord knows Sarah’s silent thoughts and asks why she laughed. Nothing is hidden from Him.

f.g: Why.

chapters.n: Here is one of the great questions of scripture: “Is any thing too hard for the LORD?” The answer, shown in Isaac’s birth, is no.

f.w: Is any thing too hard for the LORD?

chapters.n: Frightened, Sarah denies laughing. The Lord gently but firmly corrects her. He does not reject her—He simply invites honesty.

f.g: Sarah’s fear is natural; later she laughs again—this time with joy (21:6).

chapters.n: The visitors set out toward Sodom, and Abraham walks with them to see them off, as a good host would.

f.w: to bring them on the way
f.g: To escort them part of the way.

chapters.n: The Lord considers whether to share His plans with Abraham. God treats Abraham as a trusted friend.
Because Abraham will be a great nation and a blessing to all peoples, God wants him to understand His ways of justice and mercy.

f.w: all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him

chapters.n: God has chosen Abraham so he will teach his children and household to follow the Lord’s ways. Parents teaching righteousness is part of how God’s promises are fulfilled.

f.g: Righteousness and justice—doing what is right and fair.

chapters.n: An outcry has risen against Sodom and Gomorrah—perhaps the cries of their victims. Their sin is very serious.

f.g: Hebrew zeʿaqah — often the cry of the oppressed for help.

chapters.n: Like a just judge, the Lord will examine the facts before judging.

f.w: I will go down now, and see

chapters.n: Two of the men head for Sodom while Abraham remains standing before the Lord—ready to intercede.

f.g: In chapter 19 these two are called angels.

chapters.n: Abraham steps forward and boldly asks whether God will destroy the righteous along with the wicked.

f.g: To come near—language used of approaching God in prayer and worship.

chapters.n: Abraham suggests fifty righteous people. Lot and his family are surely on his mind.

f.g: Perhaps; suppose.

chapters.n: Abraham appeals to God’s own character: surely the Judge of all the earth will act justly. He prays not to change God, but in harmony with what he knows of God.

f.w: Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?

chapters.n: God agrees: for fifty righteous people He will spare the whole city. A few righteous can protect many.
Abraham humbly acknowledges he is only “dust and ashes,” yet continues to plead. Humility and boldness can go together in prayer.

f.g: A phrase of deep humility; mortal and lowly.

chapters.n: Abraham asks whether five fewer would matter. God agrees to spare it for forty-five.

f.g: Forty-five.

chapters.n: Abraham presses on to forty, and God agrees again.

f.g: For the sake of forty people.

chapters.n: Abraham, careful not to presume, asks about thirty. God again agrees.

f.w: Oh let not the Lord be angry
f.g: A respectful plea not to offend God by persistence.

chapters.n: Abraham dares to ask about twenty, and God agrees.

f.g: I have dared; I have ventured.

chapters.n: Abraham’s final request is for ten, and God agrees. The tragedy is that not even ten will be found.

f.g: Some Jewish tradition later saw ten as the minimum for a community.

chapters.n: The Lord departs, and Abraham returns home. His intercession shows the heart of a covenant person who cares for others’ salvation.

f.g: Talking intimately; conversing.

chapters.n: Two angels arrive in Sodom at evening. Lot is sitting in the city gate, where leaders and elders met—suggesting he has become a respected resident. Like Abraham, he warmly greets the strangers.

f.g: The city gate was the center of public business, legal decisions, and leadership.

chapters.n: Lot urges them to stay at his house. The angels say they will spend the night in the town square, perhaps testing Lot or the city.

f.g: Stay; remain.
Spend the night in the open square.

chapters.n: Lot insists—he knows the streets are dangerous—and serves them a meal with unleavened bread, which could be made quickly.

f.g: Strongly urged them.
Bread made without yeast, quick to prepare; later associated with the Passover deliverance.

chapters.n: Before bedtime the entire male population surrounds the house—young and old, from every part of town. The city’s corruption is complete.

f.g: Surrounded the house.

chapters.n: The mob demands the visitors so they may “know” them—meaning to sexually assault them. Violent abuse of guests violated the sacred duty of hospitality.

f.g: A Hebrew idiom for sexual relations; here it means rape.

chapters.n: Lot bravely steps outside and shuts the door behind him to protect his guests.

f.g: Lot puts himself between the mob and his guests.

chapters.n: Lot begs the men not to commit such evil, calling them “brethren” in hopes of reasoning with them.

f.g: Fellow townsmen.

chapters.n: In KJV Genesis, Lot desperately offers his daughters instead—a shocking offer that shows how deeply Sodom had warped even Lot. The Joseph Smith Translation changes this so that Lot refuses to give up his daughters.

f.g: JST Genesis 19:9-15 revises this passage: the mob seeks the daughters and Lot refuses to hand them over.

f.w: under the shadow of my roof
f.g: Under my protection as host.

chapters.n: The mob turns on Lot, mocking him as a foreigner trying to judge them. They rush forward to break down the door.

f.w: he will needs be a judge
f.g: “He wants to play the judge over us!”

chapters.n: The angels pull Lot inside and shut the door—the guests now protect their host.

f.g: Shut the door tight.

chapters.n: The angels strike the men with blindness, so they grope in vain for the door. Their spiritual blindness becomes physical.

f.g: A rare Hebrew word suggesting a sudden dazzling or confusion of sight (compare 2 Kings 6:18).

chapters.n: The angels urge Lot to gather all his family and get them out of the city.

f.g: Do you have any other family members here?

chapters.n: They reveal their mission: the Lord has sent them to destroy the city because of the great outcry against it.

f.g: Grown great.

chapters.n: Lot warns his sons-in-law, but they think he is joking. When people are steeped in the world, warnings of danger can sound ridiculous.

f.g: As if he were joking.

chapters.n: At dawn the angels urge Lot to hurry with his wife and daughters before they are swept away.

f.g: Swept away; destroyed.

chapters.n: Lot hesitates, perhaps attached to his home and possessions. The angels take the family by the hand and lead them out. The text notes this is because the Lord was merciful.

f.g: Delayed; hesitated.

f.w: the LORD being merciful unto him

chapters.n: They are told to flee to the hills without looking back or stopping. Escaping evil requires leaving it completely behind.
Lot protests, still reluctant.

f.g: “Oh no, please!”

chapters.n: Lot thanks God for saving him but fears he cannot reach the mountains safely.

f.g: Shown great kindness.

chapters.n: Lot asks to flee to a nearby small town instead. He keeps pointing out how small it is, as if a small city must hold only small sins.

f.w: is it not a little one?
f.g: Wordplay: Hebrew mitsʿar, “a little thing,” sounds like Zoar.

chapters.n: The angel grants Lot’s request and spares that town for his sake.

f.g: I have granted your request.

chapters.n: The angel urges haste; the destruction must wait until Lot is safe. The town is named Zoar, meaning “small.”

f.g: Means “small” or “insignificant”; formerly called Bela (14:2).

chapters.n: The sun has risen by the time Lot reaches Zoar.

f.g: The day of judgment dawns.

chapters.n: The Lord rains burning sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah. Some suggest an earthquake ignited the region’s tar and gas deposits, but the text stresses that the judgment came from God.

f.g: Sulfur, which burns with intense heat and a suffocating smell.

f.w: fire from the LORD out of heaven

chapters.n: The cities, the whole plain, its people, and even its plants are destroyed. Sodom becomes a lasting symbol of judgment for wickedness.
Lot’s wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. Jesus later said, “Remember Lot’s wife”—a warning against longing for a sinful past.

f.g: The Dead Sea region is still known for its salt formations.

chapters.n: Early the next morning Abraham returns to the place where he had pleaded with the Lord.

f.w: where he stood before the LORD

chapters.n: He sees smoke rising from the plain like smoke from a furnace. Not even ten righteous people were found.
God “remembered Abraham” and rescued Lot. Lot was saved largely because of Abraham’s intercession and covenant relationship with God.
Lot, now afraid to stay in Zoar, moves to the hills—where the angels first told him to go—and lives in a cave with his daughters. He has lost nearly everything.

f.g: A sad end for a man who once had flocks, herds, and a house in the city.

chapters.n: Lot’s older daughter fears they will never have husbands or children. They may have thought the destruction had been worldwide.

f.w: there is not a man in the earth
f.g: Perhaps they believed no men remained, or none would marry into their family.

chapters.n: The daughters plan to get their father drunk and have children by him. Their desperate plan shows the lasting influence of Sodom’s values.

f.g: To keep their father’s family line alive.

chapters.n: The older daughter carries out the plan while Lot is too drunk to know what is happening.

f.g: He was not aware.

chapters.n: The next day she urges her younger sister to do the same.

f.g: Last night.

chapters.n: The younger daughter follows the same plan. The account is told plainly and without approval.

f.g: The second night, repeating the wrong.

chapters.n: Both daughters become pregnant by their father.

f.g: Pregnant.

chapters.n: The older daughter’s son, Moab, becomes the ancestor of the Moabites, Israel’s neighbors east of the Dead Sea. Ruth, an ancestor of David and Jesus, was a Moabite.

f.g: Sounds like Hebrew “from father.”

chapters.n: The younger daughter’s son, Ben-ammi, becomes the ancestor of the Ammonites, another neighboring people east of the Jordan.

f.g: Means “son of my kin.”

chapters.n: Abraham moves south into the Negev and stays for a time in Gerar, a town near the coast in Philistine country.

f.g: A town in the western Negev, between Gaza and Beersheba.
Lived as a foreigner.

chapters.n: As in Egypt, Abraham says Sarah is his sister, and King Abimelech takes her into his household. The danger to the promised son’s mother is real, since Isaac is soon to be born.

f.g: Means “my father is king”; possibly a royal title used by several kings of Gerar.

chapters.n: God warns Abimelech in a dream that he is as good as dead for taking a married woman. God protects Sarah and the covenant promise.

f.w: thou art but a dead man
f.g: “You are about to die.”

chapters.n: Abimelech had not touched Sarah. He protests that he and his people are innocent.

f.g: Had relations with.

chapters.n: He explains that both Abraham and Sarah told him they were siblings, so he acted in good faith.

f.g: A clear conscience; honest intentions.
Innocent actions.

chapters.n: God agrees that Abimelech acted innocently and reveals that He kept him from sinning. God’s unseen protection guards people from wrongs they do not know they are about to commit.

f.w: I also withheld thee from sinning against me
f.g: Sin against a marriage is ultimately sin against God.
Allowed.

chapters.n: God commands Abimelech to return Sarah and calls Abraham a prophet who will pray for him—the first time the word “prophet” appears in the Bible.

f.g: First use of “prophet” (navi’) in the Bible, emphasizing intercession.

chapters.n: Abimelech wakes early and tells his officials, who are terrified. This foreign court shows more fear of God than Abraham expected.

f.g: Very afraid.

chapters.n: Abimelech confronts Abraham, asking why he brought such guilt on the kingdom. The pagan king morally rebukes the prophet.

f.g: Adultery was considered a great sin even among Israel’s neighbors.

chapters.n: Abimelech asks what Abraham was thinking.

f.g: What did you have in mind?

chapters.n: Abraham admits he assumed there was no fear of God there and feared for his life. He misjudged the people—God was at work in Gerar too.

f.g: Reverence for God that leads to moral behavior.

chapters.n: Abraham explains that Sarah is truly his half-sister—same father, different mothers. Such marriages were acceptable before the law of Moses.

f.w: the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother

chapters.n: Abraham reveals that this had been their arrangement since leaving home. The book of Abraham records that the Lord had told Abraham to say Sarai was his sister in Egypt.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — loyal love; a favor of loyalty.

chapters.n: Abimelech gives Abraham livestock and servants and returns Sarah—making generous amends.
Unlike Pharaoh, who sent Abraham away, Abimelech invites him to live anywhere in his land.

f.g: Live wherever you like.

chapters.n: Abimelech gives a large sum of silver to clear Sarah’s reputation publicly. The gift is a “covering of the eyes,” declaring she is innocent.

f.g: A very large amount—a public vindication.
A public sign of her innocence, so no one could look on her with suspicion.
Vindicated; set right.

chapters.n: Abraham prays, and God heals Abimelech’s household so they can have children again. Abraham fulfills his role as a prophet who intercedes.
The narrator explains that God had closed the wombs in Abimelech’s house. Ironically, Abraham prays for others’ fertility just before Sarah herself conceives.

f.g: Completely closed—no one could conceive.

chapters.n: At last the promise is fulfilled. The verse twice stresses that God did exactly what He said. Twenty-five years after the first promise, God keeps His word.

f.g: Came to bless; “visit” in scripture often means God’s active intervention.

chapters.n: Sarah becomes pregnant and bears a son to Abraham in their old age, right on God’s timetable.
Abraham names his son Isaac, as God instructed.

f.g: Means “he laughs.”

chapters.n: Abraham circumcises Isaac on the eighth day, faithfully keeping the covenant sign.
Abraham is a hundred years old—the birth is clearly a miracle.
Sarah’s laughter of doubt has become laughter of joy, and she invites everyone to share it.

f.w: God hath made me to laugh
f.g: Wordplay on Isaac’s name; her earlier laughter (18:12) is transformed.

chapters.n: Sarah marvels: who would have imagined she would nurse a baby? Her joyful poem celebrates the impossible made real.

f.g: Nursed children.

chapters.n: Isaac is weaned—probably around age two or three—and Abraham celebrates with a feast, marking that the child had survived the dangerous early years.

f.g: Stopped nursing; in the ancient world often at two or three years old.

chapters.n: At the feast, Sarah sees Ishmael, now a teenager, mocking or playing. The word is again a wordplay on Isaac’s name. Paul later describes Ishmael as persecuting Isaac.

f.g: Hebrew metsaḥeq — laughing, playing, or mocking; from the same root as “Isaac.”

chapters.n: Sarah demands that Hagar and Ishmael be sent away so Ishmael will not share Isaac’s inheritance.

f.g: Slave woman.

f.w: Cast out this bondwoman and her son

chapters.n: Abraham is deeply distressed. Ishmael is his son, and he loves him.

f.g: Very distressing; painful.

chapters.n: God reassures Abraham to follow Sarah’s counsel, because the covenant line will be traced through Isaac.

f.w: in Isaac shall thy seed be called

f.g: Boy; young man.

chapters.n: God promises that Ishmael, as Abraham’s son, will also become a nation. God has not forgotten him.
Early the next morning Abraham sends Hagar and Ishmael off with bread and water. They wander in the desert near Beersheba.

f.g: A waterskin made of animal hide.
A town at the northern edge of the Negev desert.

chapters.n: When the water runs out, Hagar places her son under a bush for shade, expecting him to die.

f.g: Used up.
Placed; laid down.

chapters.n: Hagar sits at a distance, unable to watch her son die, and weeps aloud. Her grief is one of scripture’s most heartrending scenes.

f.g: About the distance an arrow can fly.
Opposite him; facing him.

chapters.n: God hears the boy’s cry—fitting for a child named “God hears.” The angel comforts Hagar with “fear not.”

f.w: God heard the voice of the lad
f.g: Fulfills the meaning of Ishmael’s name.
Troubles.

chapters.n: The angel tells Hagar to lift up her son, for God will make him a great nation.

f.g: Take him firmly by the hand.

chapters.n: God opens Hagar’s eyes to see a well. Often the help we need is near, but God must open our eyes to see it.
God is with Ishmael as he grows up in the desert and becomes a skilled archer.

f.g: God’s presence and blessing continue with Ishmael.

chapters.n: Ishmael settles in the wilderness of Paran, and Hagar finds him an Egyptian wife, from her own people.

f.g: A desert in the northeastern Sinai.

chapters.n: Abimelech and his army commander approach Abraham. Even outsiders recognize that God is with Abraham.

f.w: God is with thee in all that thou doest

f.g: Army commander.

chapters.n: Abimelech asks Abraham to swear a treaty of loyalty with him and his descendants, in return for the kindness he had shown.

f.g: Act deceitfully; break faith.
Hebrew ḥesed — loyal, covenant kindness.

chapters.n: Abraham agrees to swear.

f.g: Agrees to a formal oath.

chapters.n: Abraham complains that Abimelech’s servants seized one of his wells. In dry country, wells were precious and worth fighting over.

f.g: Rebuked; complained to.

chapters.n: Abimelech says he knew nothing of it until now.

f.g: I do not know.

chapters.n: Abraham gives livestock, and the two make a covenant—a formal peace treaty.

f.g: Literally “cut a covenant.”

chapters.n: Abraham sets apart seven female lambs.

f.g: Young female sheep.

chapters.n: Abimelech asks what the seven lambs mean.

f.g: What is the meaning of these?

chapters.n: By accepting the lambs, Abimelech publicly acknowledges that Abraham dug the well—a legal witness to ownership.

f.g: Evidence or proof of an agreement.

chapters.n: The place is called Beersheba, which can mean both “well of seven” and “well of the oath.”

f.g: Hebrew sheva means “seven”; nishbaʿ means “to swear an oath.”

chapters.n: After the treaty, Abimelech and Phichol return to Philistine territory.

f.g: The narrator uses the name familiar to later readers.

chapters.n: Abraham plants a tamarisk tree in Beersheba and worships the Lord as “the everlasting God.” A long-lived tree fits the eternal God and Abraham’s settling in the land.

f.g: Hebrew ’eshel — a tamarisk tree, a hardy desert tree.
Hebrew El ʿOlam.

chapters.n: Abraham lives for a long time in Philistine territory.

f.g: Lived as a resident foreigner.

chapters.n: God tests Abraham. “Tempt” here means to test or prove, not to lure into sin. Abraham answers with ready willingness: “Here I am.”

f.g: Test or prove (Hebrew nissah). God does not entice to evil (James 1:13).
Hebrew hinneni — a reply of readiness and availability.

chapters.n: God’s command builds in painful steps: your son, your only son, Isaac, whom you love. Abraham is asked to offer the very son through whom God’s promises were to come. Latter-day Saints see this as a likeness of the Father offering His Only Begotten Son.

f.w: thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest

f.g: Later identified as the mountain where Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 3:1).

chapters.n: Abraham rises early and obeys without recorded argument. He prepares the wood himself and sets out.

f.g: A sign of prompt obedience (compare 21:14).
Split; chopped.

chapters.n: On the third day Abraham sees the place in the distance. For three days Isaac was, in Abraham’s heart, as good as dead—many see a parallel to Christ’s three days in the tomb.
Abraham tells the servants that he and the boy will worship and come back. Hebrews says Abraham believed God could raise Isaac from the dead.

f.g: Hebrew “we will return”—plural.

chapters.n: Isaac carries the wood up the mountain, as Jesus would later carry His cross. Father and son walk on together.

f.w: laid it upon Isaac his son
they went both of them together
f.g: Repeated in verse 8—father and son united in purpose.

chapters.n: Isaac asks the poignant question: “Where is the lamb?” The question echoes through scripture until John the Baptist points to Jesus.

f.w: where is the lamb for a burnt offering?

chapters.n: Abraham answers in faith: God will provide the lamb. His words point beyond the moment to the Lamb God would provide for the world.

f.w: God will provide himself a lamb
f.g: Can also be read “God will provide Himself as the lamb.”

chapters.n: Abraham builds the altar, arranges the wood, binds Isaac, and lays him on it. Isaac, likely a young man strong enough to carry wood, seems to submit willingly—like Christ.

f.g: Jewish tradition calls this story the Aqedah, “the binding.”

chapters.n: Abraham raises the knife. The text slows down to let us feel the terrible moment.

f.g: Abraham fully intends to obey.

chapters.n: The angel of the Lord calls urgently, “Abraham, Abraham!” Abraham again answers, “Here am I.”

f.g: A doubled name signals urgency and intimacy (compare Exodus 3:4; 1 Samuel 3:10).

chapters.n: The angel stops him: Abraham has proven his reverence for God by not holding back his son. God never intended Isaac’s death; human sacrifice is condemned elsewhere in scripture.

f.w: now I know that thou fearest God
Lay not thine hand upon the lad

chapters.n: Abraham sees a ram caught in a thicket and offers it in Isaac’s place. A substitute dies so the son can live—an image of Christ’s atoning sacrifice for us.

f.w: in the stead of his son
f.g: In place of his son—a picture of substitution.
Dense bushes.

chapters.n: Abraham names the place “the LORD will provide” (or “see”). The saying “in the mount of the LORD it shall be seen” anticipates the temple on this mountain and the Savior’s sacrifice nearby.

f.g: “The LORD will see” or “the LORD will provide.”

f.w: In the mount of the LORD

chapters.n: The angel calls a second time with a renewed promise.

f.g: The test is followed by blessing.

chapters.n: God swears by Himself—there is no one greater to swear by. Because Abraham did not withhold his son, the covenant is solemnly confirmed.
Abraham’s descendants will be as countless as stars and sand, and they will overcome their enemies. Latter-day revelation applies these promises to Abraham’s eternal increase.

f.w: as the stars of the heaven, and as the sand which is upon the sea shore
possess the gate of his enemies
f.g: Control their enemies’ cities—a sign of victory.

chapters.n: Through Abraham’s seed all nations will be blessed. Peter and Paul taught that this promise is fulfilled in Jesus Christ.

f.w: in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed

chapters.n: Abraham returns with Isaac to the servants, and they go home to Beersheba.
News arrives about Abraham’s brother Nahor’s family back in Mesopotamia. This short genealogy prepares for Isaac’s marriage in chapter 24.
Nahor’s sons include Huz and Buz—names linked with desert regions—and Kemuel.

f.g: The same name as Uz, Job’s homeland (Job 1:1).

chapters.n: The list continues, ending with Bethuel, the key figure for the next story.

f.g: Possibly ancestor of the Chaldeans (Kasdim).

chapters.n: Bethuel fathers Rebekah, Isaac’s future wife. Even as Abraham’s test ends, God is preparing the next step.
Nahor also has sons by a secondary wife. In total he has twelve sons—like Ishmael and Jacob after him.

f.g: A secondary wife with lower status, whose children could still be legitimate heirs.
Also the name of an Aramean region (2 Samuel 10:6).

chapters.n: Sarah dies at 127. She is the only woman in the Bible whose age at death is recorded—a mark of her honored place as mother of the covenant people.

f.w: an hundred and seven and twenty years
f.g: 127 years. Isaac would have been about 37.

chapters.n: Sarah dies in Hebron, and Abraham mourns and weeps for her. Scripture honors genuine grief; faith does not erase sorrow.

f.g: “City of Arba” (or “city of four”), an older name for Hebron.

chapters.n: Abraham rises from mourning to arrange a burial, approaching the Hittites who controlled the land.

f.g: Hittites—local people descended from Heth, son of Canaan (10:15).

chapters.n: Abraham admits he is a foreigner without land. Though God promised him all Canaan, he must ask to buy a burial plot.

f.g: A resident alien without property rights.
A respectful way of referring to burial.

chapters.n: The Hittites reply to Abraham’s request.

f.g: The local Hittite community, acting as a town council.

chapters.n: With elaborate courtesy, the Hittites call Abraham “a mighty prince” and offer him any tomb he likes. Their polite words open the bargaining.

f.g: Literally “a prince of God”—a highly respected person.
Tombs.

chapters.n: Abraham bows respectfully to the local people, showing humility and good manners.

f.g: A customary gesture of respect.

chapters.n: Abraham asks the council to speak to Ephron on his behalf—a formal, public negotiation.

f.g: Intercede for me; plead on my behalf.

chapters.n: Abraham names the property he wants—the cave of Machpelah at the edge of Ephron’s field—and insists on paying full price, so the purchase will be permanent and legal.

f.g: Machpelah may mean “double.” The traditional site is in Hebron today.

f.w: as much money as it is worth
f.g: The full price.

chapters.n: Ephron answers publicly, in the hearing of all the men at the city gate, where legal business was done.

f.g: In the hearing of.

chapters.n: Ephron offers to give the field and cave as a gift. In that culture this was likely a polite opening rather than a real gift.

f.g: Ephron offers the whole field, not just the cave—which may include obligations of ownership.

chapters.n: Abraham bows again before the people.

f.g: Abraham maintains courteous respect throughout.

chapters.n: Abraham politely refuses the gift and insists on paying. A gift could later be disputed; a purchase could not.

f.w: I will give thee money for the field

chapters.n: Ephron responds to Abraham’s offer.

f.g: The negotiation reaches its decisive point.

chapters.n: Ephron names a price of 400 shekels—“what is that between friends?” The price was quite high, but Abraham does not haggle.

f.g: About 10 pounds (4.5 kg) of silver—a large sum. Jeremiah later bought a field for 17 shekels (Jeremiah 32:9).

chapters.n: Abraham weighs out the full amount publicly, using the standard merchants’ weight. Coins did not yet exist, so silver was weighed.

f.g: Silver was weighed on scales before coins were invented.
By the standard weight accepted by traders.

chapters.n: The property is legally transferred, including the field, the cave, and every tree within its borders. The detailed list reads like a real ancient deed.

f.g: Legally confirmed; deeded.

chapters.n: The sale is confirmed before witnesses at the city gate. Abraham now legally owns his first piece of the promised land.
Abraham buries Sarah in the cave. Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah, and Jacob are later buried there too.

f.w: the cave of the field of Machpelah

chapters.n: The chapter ends by repeating that the field and cave were Abraham’s burial property. His small piece of land is a down payment on God’s larger promise.
Abraham is now very old, and the Lord has blessed him in everything. One task remains: finding a covenant wife for Isaac so the promises can continue.

f.g: Very old.

chapters.n: Abraham calls his senior servant, the manager of his household, and has him place his hand under Abraham’s thigh—a solemn way of taking an oath in that culture.

f.g: Senior or chief servant; often thought to be Eliezer (15:2), though he is unnamed here.

f.w: Put, I pray thee, thy hand under my thigh
f.g: An oath gesture near the source of life, perhaps invoking the covenant and posterity.

chapters.n: The servant must swear by the Lord not to choose a Canaanite wife for Isaac. Marrying within the covenant would preserve faith in the true God.

f.w: the God of heaven, and the God of the earth
f.g: God rules over all—not just a local deity.

f.w: not take a wife unto my son of the daughters of the Canaanites

chapters.n: Instead, he must go back to Abraham’s relatives in Mesopotamia, who shared family ties and at least some knowledge of the Lord.

f.g: The region of Haran in northern Mesopotamia.

chapters.n: The servant raises a practical concern: what if the woman refuses to come? Should Isaac move back there?

f.g: Perhaps; what if.

chapters.n: Abraham firmly says no. Isaac must not leave the promised land.

f.w: bring not my son thither again
f.g: Isaac’s future is tied to Canaan, the land of promise.

chapters.n: Abraham expresses confident faith: the God who called him and promised the land will send an angel ahead to prepare the way.

f.w: he shall send his angel before thee

chapters.n: If the woman will not come, the servant will be free from the oath—but he must never take Isaac back there.

f.g: You will be released from the obligation.

chapters.n: The servant takes the oath as Abraham asked.

f.g: Took a solemn oath.

chapters.n: The servant sets out with ten camels loaded with gifts, traveling to the city of Nahor in Mesopotamia—a journey of several hundred miles.

f.g: Hebrew Aram-naharaim, “Aram of the two rivers,” in northern Mesopotamia.
Either Haran or a town named after Abraham’s brother Nahor.

chapters.n: He arrives at the town well in the evening, when women came to draw water—a natural place to meet the town’s young women.

f.g: Fetching water was a daily task often done by young women.

chapters.n: The servant prays for success and for God to show loyal kindness to Abraham. This is the first recorded prayer for guidance in the Bible.

f.g: Grant me success.
Hebrew ḥesed — covenant loyalty and love.

chapters.n: He describes the situation to the Lord: he stands at the well as the young women come out.

f.w: the daughters of the men of the city
f.g: The young women of the town.

chapters.n: He asks for a specific sign: the right woman will offer water not only to him but to his camels. That would reveal generosity and a willing heart—a camel can drink many gallons.

f.w: I will give thy camels drink also
f.g: Watering ten thirsty camels was hard work—a sign of exceptional kindness.
Chosen; designated.

chapters.n: Before he has finished praying, Rebekah arrives—and she is Abraham’s own relative. God answers even as the prayer is offered.
Rebekah is beautiful and unmarried. She goes down to the spring and fills her jar.

f.g: Perhaps a spring reached by steps.

chapters.n: The servant runs to meet her and asks for a little water.

f.g: His eagerness shows he sees God’s hand at work.

chapters.n: Rebekah responds quickly and respectfully, lowering her jar to give him a drink.

f.g: Rebekah acts promptly—a recurring trait in this chapter.

chapters.n: Without being asked, she offers to water all his camels until they are satisfied—exactly the sign he prayed for.

f.g: Ten camels could drink well over a hundred gallons.

chapters.n: Rebekah runs back and forth, emptying her jar into the trough and drawing more, until all the camels have had enough.

f.g: A drinking basin for animals.

chapters.n: The servant watches silently, wondering whether this is truly the Lord’s answer.

f.g: Remained silent.
To know; to find out.

chapters.n: When the camels finish, he gives her a gold nose ring and two heavy gold bracelets—signs of Abraham’s wealth and the seriousness of his mission.

f.g: A nose ring (see verse 47).
About 4 ounces (115 grams) of gold.

chapters.n: He asks whose daughter she is and whether there is room to stay the night.

f.g: Spend the night.

chapters.n: Rebekah names her father and grandparents—Abraham’s relatives. The servant’s prayer is fully answered.
She adds that there is plenty of straw, feed, and room. Her hospitality matches Abraham’s.

f.g: Animal feed.

chapters.n: The servant bows and worships the Lord. Gratitude is his first response to answered prayer.
He praises the Lord for His steadfast kindness and faithfulness. “I being in the way, the LORD led me” is a lovely model: keep moving in faith, and God guides.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed and ’emet — loyal love and faithfulness, a frequent pair in scripture.

f.w: I being in the way, the LORD led me

chapters.n: Rebekah runs home and tells her mother’s household everything.

f.g: The women’s quarters of the household.

chapters.n: Her brother Laban runs out to the well to meet the man. Laban will play a big role in Jacob’s story later.

f.g: Means “white.”

chapters.n: Laban’s interest is sparked when he sees the gold jewelry. The narrator hints at Laban’s love of wealth, which shows again in Jacob’s day.

f.w: when he saw the earring and bracelets

chapters.n: Laban warmly welcomes the servant as one “blessed of the LORD,” saying the house and stable are ready.

f.g: Laban uses the name of the Lord, showing the family knew of Him.

chapters.n: The servant is welcomed in. The camels are unloaded and fed, and water is brought to wash the travelers’ feet.

f.g: Unloaded; unharnessed.

chapters.n: Food is served, but the servant refuses to eat until he explains his errand. Duty comes before comfort.

f.g: Food.
Mission; business.

chapters.n: He introduces himself simply as Abraham’s servant. He never gives his own name—his identity is in serving his master.

f.g: The servant remains unnamed throughout the chapter.

chapters.n: He tells how the Lord has made Abraham wealthy—essentially presenting Isaac’s family as a good match.

f.w: the LORD hath blessed my master greatly

chapters.n: Sarah bore a son in her old age, and Abraham has given him everything. Isaac is the sole heir.

f.w: unto him hath he given all that he hath

chapters.n: He explains the oath: Isaac must not marry a Canaanite.
He must find a wife from Abraham’s own family.

f.g: Abraham’s family clan.

chapters.n: He recounts his own question: what if the woman will not come?

f.w: Peradventure the woman will not follow me

chapters.n: He repeats Abraham’s faith that an angel would guide him. Retelling the story lets the family see God’s hand at every step.

f.g: Whom I serve and live in obedience to.

chapters.n: He explains that he would be freed from the oath if the family refused.
He describes arriving at the well and praying to Abraham’s God for success.

f.w: if now thou do prosper my way
f.g: If you will now make my journey succeed.

chapters.n: He repeats the sign he asked for: a young woman who would offer him water.

f.g: Here, the young unmarried woman.

chapters.n: …and who would also offer to water his camels. That woman would be the Lord’s choice.

f.g: Chosen; marked out.

chapters.n: He tells how Rebekah appeared even before he finished praying silently in his heart.

f.g: He had prayed silently—God hears unspoken prayers.

chapters.n: Rebekah did exactly what he had asked of the Lord.

f.g: Hurried.

chapters.n: He describes asking about her family and giving her the jewelry.

f.g: A nose ring.

chapters.n: He bowed and worshipped the Lord, who led him to his master’s relative. His account gives God all the credit.

f.w: led me in the right way

chapters.n: He asks for a clear answer: will the family deal kindly and truly with Abraham? Either way, he needs to know where to go next.

f.g: Show loyal kindness and faithfulness—echoing verse 27.

f.w: turn to the right hand, or to the left
f.g: Decide on his next move.

chapters.n: Laban and Bethuel recognize the matter comes from the Lord. They cannot argue with it.

f.w: we cannot speak unto thee bad or good
f.g: We cannot say anything one way or the other.

chapters.n: They agree: Rebekah may go to become Isaac’s wife, as the Lord has directed.

f.g: They accept the outcome as God’s will.

chapters.n: The servant bows to the ground in worship again. Each step of the journey is marked by gratitude.

f.g: A posture of deep reverence.

chapters.n: He gives Rebekah jewelry and clothing, and gifts to her brother and mother—customary betrothal gifts.

f.g: Clothing.
Valuable gifts, perhaps part of a bride-price.

chapters.n: After a night of feasting, the servant asks to leave right away.

f.g: Stayed.

f.w: a few days, at the least ten
f.g: Possibly “days or ten,” a vague period, perhaps much longer.

chapters.n: The servant asks them not to delay him, since the Lord has made the journey succeed.

chapters.n: The family decides to let Rebekah decide for herself.

f.g: Ask her directly.

chapters.n: Rebekah answers simply: “I will go.” Like Abraham before her, she leaves home and family by faith for a land she has never seen.

f.g: Deborah, who later dies near Bethel (35:8).

chapters.n: Her family blesses her to become the mother of countless descendants who will overcome their enemies—remarkably echoing God’s promise to Abraham.

f.g: Literally “thousands of ten thousands”—a vast number.

f.w: possess the gate of those which hate them

chapters.n: Rebekah and her maids mount the camels and follow the servant home.

f.g: Her young female attendants.

chapters.n: Meanwhile Isaac has come from Beer-lahai-roi, where he lives in the Negev.

f.g: The well where God appeared to Hagar.

chapters.n: Isaac goes out in the evening to meditate in the field. As he looks up, he sees the camels approaching.

f.g: The Hebrew is uncertain—perhaps to pray, ponder, or walk.
Evening.

chapters.n: Rebekah looks up, sees Isaac, and quickly gets down from her camel.

f.g: Got down from; dismounted.

chapters.n: Learning the man is Isaac, she covers herself with a veil, as a bride customarily did.

f.g: A bride wore a veil before the wedding (compare 29:23-25).

chapters.n: The servant tells Isaac everything that happened—another testimony of God’s guidance.

f.g: The servant’s report completes his faithful mission.

chapters.n: Isaac brings Rebekah into Sarah’s tent, marries her, and loves her. Isaac is comforted after his mother’s death. This is the first time the Bible says a husband loved his wife.

f.g: The first mention of a husband’s love for his wife in scripture.

chapters.n: Abraham takes another wife, Keturah. Whether this happened after Sarah’s death or earlier is not clear; 1 Chronicles calls her a concubine.

f.g: Her name may mean “incense.”

chapters.n: Keturah bears six sons, ancestors of Arabian desert tribes. Most notable is Midian, ancestor of the Midianites.

f.g: The Midianites included Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, from whom Moses received the priesthood.

chapters.n: Jokshan’s descendants include Sheba and Dedan, names of Arabian trading peoples.
Midian’s sons are listed. Ephah later appears as a people known for camels and trade.
Abraham leaves his entire estate to Isaac, the covenant heir.
Abraham gives gifts to his other sons and sends them east, away from Isaac, so there would be no dispute over the inheritance. He provides for all his children.

f.g: Secondary wives—here Hagar and Keturah.
The lands east of Canaan, toward Arabia.

chapters.n: Abraham lives 175 years—a full century after he first left Haran.

f.w: an hundred threescore and fifteen years
f.g: 175 years (a “score” is twenty).

chapters.n: Abraham dies peacefully, satisfied with life, and is “gathered to his people.” This phrase suggests joining his ancestors beyond death, hinting at life after death.

f.g: Breathed his last; died. “Ghost” means spirit.

chapters.n: Isaac and Ishmael bury their father together. Abraham’s death brings his estranged sons together.

f.g: A touching reunion of half-brothers.

chapters.n: Abraham is buried with Sarah in the field he bought—his only owned piece of the promised land.

f.w: there was Abraham buried, and Sarah his wife

chapters.n: God blesses Isaac after Abraham’s death. The covenant passes to the next generation.

Ishmael’s sons are named. Nebajoth and Kedar became well-known Arabian tribes.

f.g: A powerful Arabian tribe often mentioned by the prophets (Isaiah 21:16; Psalms 120:5).

chapters.n: More of Ishmael’s sons, linked with oases and regions of Arabia.

f.g: Perhaps the oasis of Dumat al-Jandal in northern Arabia.

chapters.n: The list continues, completing twelve sons.

f.g: An important oasis in northwestern Arabia (Job 6:19).

chapters.n: Ishmael has twelve sons who become tribal princes, just as God promised—a parallel to Jacob’s twelve sons.

f.g: Encampments or fortified settlements.

chapters.n: Ishmael lives 137 years and dies, joining his ancestors.
Ishmael’s descendants spread across the desert between Egypt and Mesopotamia, living alongside—and sometimes in tension with—their relatives, just as foretold.

f.w: in the presence of all his brethren

f.g: The desert region near Egypt’s eastern border.

chapters.n: Isaac’s family story now begins.

f.g: A new major section of Genesis begins (toledot).

chapters.n: Isaac married Rebekah at forty. She came from Paddan-aram, “the plain of Aram,” in northern Mesopotamia.

f.g: The region around Haran in northern Mesopotamia.
An Aramean.

chapters.n: Like Sarah, Rebekah cannot have children. Isaac prays earnestly for her, and the Lord answers. The covenant line repeatedly depends on God’s miracles, not human strength.

f.g: Prayed earnestly; pleaded.

chapters.n: The twins struggle within her, and Rebekah, troubled, goes to ask the Lord herself. She seeks personal revelation.

f.g: Literally “why this, I?”—an expression of distress.

f.w: she went to inquire of the LORD

chapters.n: The Lord reveals to Rebekah that two nations are in her womb and that the elder will serve the younger. This revelation shapes her later actions.

f.w: the elder shall serve the younger

f.g: Israel (from Jacob) and Edom (from Esau).

chapters.n: When the time comes, she gives birth to twins.

f.w: her days to be delivered were fulfilled
f.g: Her time to give birth arrived.

chapters.n: The first baby is red and covered with hair, so they name him Esau. These details anticipate his later names and homeland.

f.g: Hebrew ’admoni—a wordplay on Edom (“red”).
Hebrew seʿar—a wordplay on Seir, Edom’s mountain homeland.

chapters.n: The second baby comes out gripping his brother’s heel, so he is named Jacob. Isaac is sixty when the twins are born—twenty years after his marriage.

f.g: Sounds like Hebrew ʿaqev, “heel”; it can mean “he grasps the heel” or “he supplants.”
Sixty.

chapters.n: The twins grow into very different men: Esau an outdoorsman and skilled hunter, Jacob a quiet man who stays near the tents.

f.g: Skillful.
Hebrew tam—quiet, settled, even “whole” or “blameless”; the same word used of Job.

chapters.n: Isaac favors Esau for the game he brings home; Rebekah favors Jacob. Parental favoritism plants seeds of conflict.

f.g: Wild game, not just deer.

chapters.n: Jacob is cooking stew when Esau comes in from the field, exhausted and starving.

f.g: Boiled; cooked.
A thick soup or stew.
Exhausted; weak with hunger.

chapters.n: Esau demands some of the “red stuff.” His coarse words reveal his appetite, and earn him the nickname Edom, “red.”

f.g: Literally “that red, that red stuff”—Esau seems too hungry even to name it.
Means “red.”

chapters.n: Jacob seizes the moment to ask for Esau’s birthright—the firstborn’s rights of leadership and a double inheritance.

f.g: The firstborn son’s privileges: leadership of the family and a double portion of inheritance.

chapters.n: Esau exaggerates his need and shrugs off the birthright as useless. He values a meal more than his spiritual heritage.

f.w: what profit shall this birthright do to me?
f.g: “What good is a birthright to me?”

chapters.n: Jacob insists that Esau swear an oath, and Esau sells the birthright.

f.g: An oath made the transfer binding.

chapters.n: Esau eats, drinks, gets up, and leaves—four quick verbs that show his careless attitude. The narrator concludes that Esau “despised” his birthright. Hebrews uses him as a warning against trading eternal blessings for momentary desires.

f.g: Lentils.

chapters.n: Another famine strikes, as in Abraham’s day, and Isaac moves to Gerar under King Abimelech. Isaac’s life often echoes his father’s, showing the same God guiding a new generation.

f.w: the first famine that was in the days of Abraham

f.g: Possibly a royal title or a later king of the same name as in chapter 20.

chapters.n: The Lord appears to Isaac and tells him not to go to Egypt but to stay where God directs. Isaac, unlike Abraham and Jacob, never leaves the promised land.

f.g: Isaac remains in the land of promise all his life.

chapters.n: God promises to be with Isaac, bless him, give him the land, and fulfill the oath He swore to Abraham. The covenant is now Isaac’s.

f.w: the oath which I sware unto Abraham

chapters.n: God repeats the covenant promises to Isaac: countless descendants, the land, and blessing for all nations.

f.w: in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed

f.w: my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws
f.g: A full list of terms for God’s instructions, stressing Abraham’s complete obedience.

chapters.n: Isaac settles in Gerar.

f.g: Lived; stayed.

chapters.n: Like his father, Isaac fears for his life and says his beautiful wife is his sister. Unlike Sarah, Rebekah was his cousin, not his sister.

f.g: Caressing or laughing with; another wordplay on Isaac’s name (“he laughs”).

chapters.n: Abimelech confronts Isaac, who admits he feared for his life.

f.g: Certainly; surely.

f.g: Easily.
Lain; had relations.

chapters.n: Abimelech orders protection for Isaac and Rebekah under penalty of death. God turns Isaac’s fearful mistake into safety.

f.g: Commanded.

chapters.n: Isaac plants crops and harvests a hundred times what he sowed—an extraordinary yield in a famine. The Lord blesses him.
Isaac grows richer and richer until he is very wealthy.

f.g: Grew great; became prosperous.

chapters.n: His wealth in livestock and servants makes the Philistines jealous.

f.g: Were jealous of.

f.g: Blocked; filled in.

chapters.n: Abimelech asks Isaac to leave because he has become too powerful.

f.g: More powerful; more numerous.

chapters.n: Isaac moves peacefully to the valley of Gerar rather than fight.

f.g: Hebrew naḥal—a wadi or streambed that flows only in the rainy season.

chapters.n: Isaac re-digs his father’s wells and gives them the names Abraham had used. He honors and restores his father’s legacy.

f.g: Many see a parallel to restoring old truths—reopening wells of living water.

chapters.n: Isaac’s servants dig and find a well of fresh, running water.

f.g: Literally “living water”—fresh water from a spring.

chapters.n: The local herdsmen claim the water. Isaac names the well Esek, “quarrel.”

f.g: Means “contention” or “quarrel.”

chapters.n: They dig another well, and that one too is disputed. Isaac names it Sitnah, “opposition.”

f.g: Means “hostility” or “accusation”; related to the word “Satan.”

f.g: Means “wide places” or “room.”

f.w: the LORD hath made room for us

f.w: I am the God of Abraham thy father

f.g: Why.

f.w: thou art now the blessed of the LORD
f.g: An acknowledgment of God’s favor on Isaac.

f.g: Early.

chapters.n: That same day his servants report that they have found water—a sign of God’s approval of the peace.

f.g: A timely blessing right after making peace.

f.g: The same age at which Isaac married (25:20).

chapters.n: Isaac senses he may die soon. (He actually lives many more years—35:28.)

chapters.n: He asks Esau to hunt game for him.

f.g: A case for carrying arrows.
Wild game.

f.g: Rebekah acts quickly and decisively.

f.g: In the Lord’s presence; a solemn religious act.

f.g: Repeated in verses 13 and 43—Rebekah takes responsibility.

chapters.n: She asks for two young goats so she can cook a dish just as Isaac likes.

f.g: Young goats.

chapters.n: Jacob is to bring the meal to Isaac and receive the blessing.

f.g: The blessing carried the covenant birthright already sold to Jacob (25:33).

chapters.n: Jacob gets the goats, and Rebekah prepares the meal.

f.g: Brought.

chapters.n: Rebekah hands Jacob the food and bread.

f.w: into the hand of her son Jacob
f.g: The plan now depends on Jacob.

f.g: Isaac’s question shows his suspicion from the start.

chapters.n: Isaac asks how he found game so quickly. Jacob even invokes God in his answer.

f.g: A famous line expressing a contradiction between appearance and reality.

chapters.n: Isaac eats and drinks the meal Jacob brings.

f.g: Part of the formal meal.

chapters.n: Isaac asks his son to come and kiss him.

f.g: A gesture of affection—and a final test by scent.

chapters.n: He blesses him to rule over nations and over his own brothers, and repeats the Abrahamic promise: those who curse him will be cursed and those who bless him blessed.

chapters.n: Esau prepares his dish and brings it in, asking for the blessing.

f.g: Esau speaks with confidence, unaware.

f.g: He plans to wait until after Isaac’s death and funeral.
