f.g: Called Bashemath in Genesis 36:3.

chapters.n: Jacob sets out alone from Beersheba toward Haran, a journey of about 500 miles. He flees with little, unlike Abraham’s servant who traveled with ten camels.
At sunset he stops at a certain place and sleeps outdoors with a stone for a headrest. He is alone, vulnerable, and far from home.

f.g: Came upon; arrived at.
Literally “the place”—hinting it is a special, sacred spot.

chapters.n: Jacob dreams of a stairway reaching from earth to heaven with angels going up and down. Heaven and earth are connected. Jesus later applied this image to Himself, and many Latter-day Saints see in it the steps of temple covenants leading back to God.

f.g: Hebrew sullam—a stairway or ramp, perhaps like the stepped sides of a ziggurat.

chapters.n: The Lord stands above the stairway and introduces Himself as the God of Abraham and Isaac. He promises Jacob the land on which he lies.

f.g: Or “stood beside him.”

f.w: the LORD God of Abraham thy father, and the God of Isaac

chapters.n: God renews the Abrahamic covenant with Jacob: countless descendants spreading in every direction, and blessing for all the world’s families through him.

f.w: as the dust of the earth
in thy seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed

chapters.n: God promises to be with Jacob everywhere, protect him, bring him home, and never leave him. These words would sustain Jacob through twenty hard years.

f.g: Watch over and protect.

chapters.n: Jacob wakes in awe: the Lord was here, and he had not realized it. God can meet us in unexpected places.

f.w: Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not
f.g: A moment of spiritual awakening.

chapters.n: Filled with reverent fear, Jacob calls the place the house of God and gate of heaven—the essence of what a temple is.

f.g: Awesome; awe-inspiring—not terrible.
Hebrew Bet-’El.
Ironically what Babel claimed to be (Bab-ili, “gate of god”); here God Himself provides it.

chapters.n: Early in the morning Jacob sets up his stone as a pillar and anoints it with oil, consecrating the place as holy.

f.g: A standing stone set up as a memorial.

f.w: poured oil upon the top of it
f.g: Anointing dedicated something to God.

chapters.n: He names the place Bethel, “house of God”; the town nearby was called Luz.

f.g: “House of God.”
Possibly “almond tree.”

chapters.n: Jacob makes a vow: if God protects him and provides food and clothing on his journey…

f.g: Made a solemn promise to God.

f.w: bread to eat, and raiment to put on

chapters.n: …and brings him safely home, then the Lord will be his God. Jacob’s “if” may reflect early, growing faith—or a humble acceptance of God’s own promises.

f.w: then shall the LORD be my God

chapters.n: Jacob promises that the stone will mark God’s house and that he will give God a tenth of all he receives—following Abraham’s example of tithing.

f.w: I will surely give the tenth unto thee

chapters.n: Strengthened by his vision at Bethel, Jacob continues to “the land of the people of the east,” the region of Haran.

f.g: Literally “lifted up his feet”—suggesting renewed energy after Bethel.
Peoples east of Canaan, here the Arameans of Mesopotamia.

chapters.n: Jacob comes to a well in a field where three flocks are waiting. A large stone covers the well to protect the precious water.

f.g: Wells are frequent meeting places for future spouses in scripture (24:11; Exodus 2:15-21).

chapters.n: The shepherds wait until all the flocks gather, then roll away the heavy stone together, water the sheep, and replace it.

f.g: The stone apparently needed several men to move.

chapters.n: Jacob asks where they are from. “Haran,” they say—he has arrived.

f.g: A friendly greeting, “friends.”

chapters.n: He asks whether they know Laban, Nahor’s grandson.

f.g: “Son” here means descendant; Laban was Nahor’s grandson (24:29).

chapters.n: They say Laban is well—and here comes his daughter Rachel with the sheep. Providence is at work again.

f.g: Literally “Is there peace (shalom) to him?”
Means “ewe”—fitting for a shepherdess.

chapters.n: Jacob suggests they water the sheep and send them back to graze, since it is still midday. Perhaps he hopes for privacy with Rachel.

f.g: It is still the middle of the day.

chapters.n: The shepherds explain the custom: they wait until all the flocks arrive to move the stone.

f.g: Custom or agreement required them to wait.

chapters.n: Rachel arrives with her father’s flock; she is a shepherdess.

f.g: She tended them.

chapters.n: Seeing Rachel, Jacob single-handedly rolls the stone away and waters Laban’s flock. His strength and eagerness show his excitement.

f.w: rolled the stone from the well's mouth
f.g: Jacob does alone what normally took several men.

chapters.n: Jacob kisses Rachel—a family greeting—and weeps aloud with emotion. After a long, lonely journey, he has found family.

f.g: A customary greeting between relatives.

chapters.n: Jacob explains he is her relative, Rebekah’s son. Rachel runs to tell her father.

f.g: Here “brother” means relative; Jacob was Laban’s nephew.

chapters.n: Laban runs to meet Jacob, embraces him, and brings him home. He once ran out for Abraham’s servant too—though now Jacob brings no camels laden with gold.
Laban acknowledges Jacob as his own flesh and blood. Jacob stays a month, presumably working for him.

f.g: My own family.

chapters.n: Laban offers to pay Jacob, appearing generous—but he is also making Jacob an employee rather than family.

f.g: For nothing; without pay.

chapters.n: Laban has two daughters: Leah, the elder, and Rachel, the younger.

f.g: Possibly “cow” or “weary.”

chapters.n: Leah had “tender” eyes, while Rachel was beautiful in form and face.

f.g: Hebrew rakkot—soft, delicate, or weak; the meaning is uncertain and may be a compliment.
Good-looking.

chapters.n: Jacob loves Rachel and offers seven years of labor as a bride-price, since he has no wealth to give.

f.w: I will serve thee seven years
f.g: A generous offer; bride-prices were often paid in goods.

chapters.n: Laban agrees in vague terms—it is better for her to marry family than an outsider.

f.g: Stay with me.

chapters.n: Jacob works seven years, and they feel like only a few days because of his love for Rachel. One of the Bible’s most beautiful descriptions of love.

f.w: they seemed unto him but a few days
f.g: Love makes long service feel light.

chapters.n: When the seven years end, Jacob asks for his bride.

f.g: My term of service is complete.

chapters.n: Laban throws a wedding feast for the whole town.

f.g: A wedding banquet, often with much wine.

chapters.n: That evening Laban brings Leah instead of Rachel. In the darkness and with the bride veiled, Jacob does not realize it.

f.g: Darkness and veiling made the switch possible.

chapters.n: Laban gives Leah his servant Zilpah as her maid—a customary wedding gift.
Morning reveals Leah. Jacob protests that he was deceived. The deceiver has been deceived—the elder substituted for the younger, just as Jacob once posed as the elder.

f.g: Deceived; tricked.

chapters.n: Laban claims local custom: the younger daughter cannot marry before the firstborn. His words sting, given Jacob’s own history with the firstborn’s rights.

f.g: Laban’s word choice echoes Jacob’s deception of his father.

chapters.n: Laban offers Rachel too after the week-long wedding celebration—if Jacob works seven more years.

f.g: Complete the seven-day wedding celebration with Leah.

chapters.n: Jacob agrees, finishes the week, and marries Rachel as well.

f.g: Jacob now has two wives who are sisters—later forbidden in the law of Moses (Leviticus 18:18).

chapters.n: Laban gives Rachel his servant Bilhah as her maid.
Jacob loves Rachel more than Leah and serves seven more years. Favoritism again sows trouble in the family.

f.w: loved also Rachel more than Leah
f.g: The family pattern of favoritism continues (25:28; 37:3).

chapters.n: The Lord sees that Leah is unloved and opens her womb, while Rachel remains childless. God notices and cares for the overlooked.

f.g: A Hebrew idiom meaning “loved less,” not necessarily active hatred.

chapters.n: Leah names her first son Reuben, hoping her husband will now love her. Each name reveals the ache of her heart.

f.g: Sounds like “See, a son!” and “the LORD has seen my affliction.”

chapters.n: Her second son is Simeon, because the Lord “heard” she was unloved.

f.g: From Hebrew shamaʿ, “to hear.”

chapters.n: Her third son is Levi, hoping her husband will now be “joined” to her. Levi’s descendants will become Israel’s priestly tribe.

f.g: Sounds like Hebrew lawah, “joined” or “attached.”

chapters.n: With her fourth son, Leah’s focus shifts: “Now will I praise the LORD.” She names him Judah. From Judah come King David and Jesus Christ.

f.g: Related to Hebrew yadah, “to praise.”

chapters.n: Rachel, still childless, envies her sister and cries to Jacob in desperation. Her pain is real, though her demand is unfair.

f.w: Give me children, or else I die
f.g: Tragically, Rachel later dies giving birth to her second son (35:16-19).

chapters.n: Jacob angrily replies that he is not God—only God gives children. He is right, but his answer lacks compassion; contrast Isaac, who prayed for Rebekah.

f.g: “Am I in the place of God?”

chapters.n: Rachel offers her maid Bilhah, following the same custom Sarah used. A child born “upon her knees” would count as Rachel’s own.

f.g: A ritual of adoption: the child would be born onto Rachel’s lap and counted as hers.

f.w: that I may also have children by her

chapters.n: Rachel gives Bilhah to Jacob as a wife.

f.g: As a secondary wife; her children were full sons of Jacob.

chapters.n: Bilhah conceives and bears a son.

f.g: Jacob’s fifth son.

chapters.n: Rachel names him Dan, believing God has judged her case and heard her plea.

f.g: Means “he judged” or “vindicated.”

chapters.n: Bilhah bears a second son.

f.g: Jacob’s sixth son.

chapters.n: Rachel names him Naphtali, saying she has wrestled with her sister and won. The rivalry between the sisters is intense.

f.g: From Hebrew for “my wrestling.”
Literally “wrestlings of God”—mighty struggles.

chapters.n: Leah, no longer having children, gives her maid Zilpah to Jacob as well. The competition escalates.

f.g: Stopped having children.

chapters.n: Zilpah bears a son.

f.g: Jacob’s seventh son.

chapters.n: Leah names him Gad, meaning good fortune.

f.g: Better “Good fortune has come!”
Means “fortune” or “luck.”

chapters.n: Zilpah bears a second son.

f.g: Jacob’s eighth son.

chapters.n: Leah names him Asher, “happy,” saying women will call her blessed.

f.g: Means “happy” or “blessed.”

chapters.n: Reuben finds mandrakes during the wheat harvest and brings them to his mother. Rachel asks for some, likely believing they would help her conceive.

f.g: A plant with a fragrant fruit, believed in the ancient world to promote fertility (compare Song of Solomon 7:13).
Around May–June.

chapters.n: Leah bitterly says Rachel has already taken her husband. Rachel strikes a bargain: Jacob will spend the night with Leah in exchange for the mandrakes.

f.g: “Isn’t it enough that…?”

chapters.n: Leah meets Jacob and tells him she has “hired” him for the night. The household’s rivalry is painfully on display.

f.g: Paid for; a wordplay on Issachar’s name in verse 18.

chapters.n: God listens to Leah, and she bears a fifth son. Ironically, it is Leah—who gave away the mandrakes—who conceives. Children come from God, not from charms.

f.g: God answers Leah’s prayers.

chapters.n: Leah names him Issachar, meaning “reward” or “hire.”

f.g: Sounds like Hebrew “there is a reward (sakar).”
Wages; reward.

chapters.n: Leah bears a sixth son.

f.g: Leah’s sixth son, Jacob’s tenth.

chapters.n: She names him Zebulun, hoping her husband will now honor or dwell with her. Leah still longs for Jacob’s love.

f.g: Endowed; given.
Sounds like Hebrew zaval, “to honor” or “to dwell.”

chapters.n: Leah also bears a daughter, Dinah. She is the only daughter named, because her story comes later (chapter 34).

f.g: Means “judgment” or “vindicated,” a feminine form related to Dan.

chapters.n: At last God remembers Rachel and answers her prayers. After years of waiting, her womb is opened.
Rachel bears a son and says God has taken away her shame. In that culture, childlessness was often wrongly seen as a disgrace.

f.g: My disgrace or shame.

chapters.n: She names him Joseph, praying the Lord will “add” another son. Joseph will become one of the Bible’s great heroes, and Latter-day Saints treasure the promises to his descendants, including the Nephites.

f.g: Means “may He add”; also sounds like “He has taken away.”

chapters.n: After Joseph’s birth—and the end of his fourteen years of service—Jacob asks Laban to let him go home.

f.g: His homeland of Canaan.

chapters.n: Jacob asks for his wives and children, reminding Laban of his faithful service.

f.w: for whom I have served thee

chapters.n: Laban urges Jacob to stay, admitting he has learned through divination that the Lord blessed him because of Jacob.

f.g: Hebrew niḥashti—“I have learned by divination,” suggesting Laban used omens.

f.w: the LORD hath blessed me for thy sake

chapters.n: Laban invites Jacob to name his wages.

f.g: Name your price.

chapters.n: Jacob reminds Laban how faithfully he has worked and cared for his livestock.

f.w: how thy cattle was with me
f.g: How your herds fared under my care.

chapters.n: Laban’s small flock has multiplied under Jacob’s care. Now Jacob wants to build up his own household.

f.g: Literally “at my foot”—wherever Jacob went.

chapters.n: Jacob asks for no wages up front. He proposes a deal instead.

f.w: Thou shalt not give me any thing
f.g: Jacob asks for nothing in advance.

chapters.n: Jacob’s wages will be the unusually colored animals: speckled and spotted goats and dark sheep. Most sheep there were white and most goats dark, so this seemed a small share.

f.g: Animals with irregular coloring—normally a minority.

chapters.n: Jacob’s honesty will be easy to check: any plain-colored animal found in his flock could be counted as stolen.

f.g: My honesty.

chapters.n: Laban agrees eagerly, sure he is getting the better deal.

f.w: I would it might be according to thy word
f.g: “Agreed—let it be as you say.”

chapters.n: That same day Laban secretly removes all the spotted and dark animals and gives them to his sons—cheating Jacob from the start.

f.g: Striped or banded.

chapters.n: Laban puts three days’ distance between his sons’ flocks and Jacob, so the spotted animals cannot breed with Jacob’s flock.

f.g: A long distance—perhaps 50 miles or more.

chapters.n: Jacob peels white stripes into branches of poplar, almond, and plane trees.

f.g: Peeled white stripes in the bark.
Probably almond (luz)—a wordplay with Bethel’s old name, Luz.
Probably the plane tree.

chapters.n: He places the striped branches at the watering troughs where the animals mated.

f.g: Watering channels or troughs.

chapters.n: The flocks bear striped and spotted young. Ancient people believed what animals saw could affect their offspring; Jacob later credits God’s revelation, not the sticks, for the result (31:10-12).
Jacob separates his flock and positions Laban’s animals to face his striped ones, building up his own herds.

f.w: set the faces of the flocks
f.g: Arranged the flocks so they faced the striped animals.

chapters.n: Jacob uses the branches only when the strongest animals breed.

f.g: The healthiest, most vigorous animals.

chapters.n: The weaker animals go to Laban and the stronger to Jacob. Jacob uses selective breeding to his advantage.

f.g: Weak.

chapters.n: Jacob becomes very wealthy with flocks, servants, camels, and donkeys. Despite Laban’s schemes, God prospers Jacob as He promised at Bethel.
Laban’s sons complain that Jacob has grown rich at their father’s expense. Jealousy is turning the household against Jacob.

f.g: Wealth; literally “weight” or “heaviness.”

chapters.n: Jacob notices that Laban’s attitude toward him has changed. The relationship has soured.

f.g: Face; expression.

chapters.n: The Lord tells Jacob to return home and promises, “I will be with thee”—the same promise made at Bethel.
Jacob calls Rachel and Leah out to the field, where they can speak privately.

f.g: Away from Laban’s household, to talk in private.

chapters.n: Jacob explains that Laban has turned against him, but God has stayed with him.

f.w: the God of my father hath been with me

chapters.n: Jacob reminds his wives how hard he has worked for their father.

f.g: With all my strength.

chapters.n: Laban cheated him by changing his wages again and again, but God protected him.

f.g: A Hebrew expression meaning “many times” or “over and over.”
Did not allow him.

chapters.n: Whatever terms Laban set, the flocks produced in Jacob’s favor. God overruled Laban’s schemes.

f.g: Striped.

chapters.n: Jacob gives God the credit for transferring Laban’s flocks to him.

f.w: God hath taken away the cattle of your father
f.g: Jacob sees God’s hand, not his own cleverness, behind his wealth.

chapters.n: Jacob recounts a dream at breeding time showing the rams were striped and spotted.

f.g: Grizzled; dappled or mottled.

chapters.n: The angel of God called Jacob by name, and he answered, “Here am I,” like Abraham before him.
The angel showed Jacob that God had seen Laban’s mistreatment and was blessing Jacob’s flock. The striped branches of chapter 30 were not the real cause.

f.w: I have seen all that Laban doeth unto thee

chapters.n: God identifies Himself as the God of Bethel, reminding Jacob of his vow there, and tells him to go home.
Rachel and Leah agree: there is nothing left for them in their father’s house. For once the sisters speak with one voice.

f.g: A share of the family estate.

chapters.n: They complain that Laban treated them like foreigners, “selling” them and using up the bride-price that should have benefited them.

f.g: Spent the wealth (from Jacob’s labor) that should have been their dowry.

chapters.n: They affirm that the wealth God gave Jacob belongs to them and their children, and they urge him to obey God.

f.w: whatsoever God hath said unto thee, do

chapters.n: Jacob loads his family onto camels.

f.g: Acted at once.

chapters.n: He takes all the livestock and property he earned in Paddan-aram and sets off to his father Isaac in Canaan.

f.g: The livestock he had earned.

chapters.n: While Laban is away shearing sheep, Rachel steals her father’s household idols. These figurines may have represented family gods or even claims to inheritance.

f.g: Hebrew teraphim—household idols or figurines, perhaps tied to family protection or inheritance rights.
Sheep-shearing was a busy, festive time that took the men away.

chapters.n: Jacob slips away without telling Laban.

f.g: Literally “stole the heart of”—deceived; left secretly.

chapters.n: Jacob crosses the Euphrates and heads toward the hill country of Gilead, east of the Jordan.

f.g: The Euphrates.
A hilly, wooded region east of the Jordan River.

chapters.n: Laban learns on the third day that Jacob has fled.

f.g: Jacob has a head start.

chapters.n: Laban gathers his relatives and chases Jacob for seven days, catching up in Gilead.

f.g: His kinsmen.

chapters.n: God warns Laban in a dream not to say anything to Jacob, good or bad. God protects Jacob as promised.

f.g: An idiom: do nothing at all to harm him.

chapters.n: Laban catches up, and both camps pitch tents in the hills of Gilead.

f.g: Set up camp in the hill country.

chapters.n: Laban accuses Jacob of carrying off his daughters like prisoners of war.

f.g: Like spoils of war.

chapters.n: He claims he would have sent them off with a farewell celebration—music, songs, tambourines, and harps. His claim of warm intentions sounds hollow.

f.g: A small drum or tambourine.
Joyful celebration.

chapters.n: Laban complains that he did not even get to kiss his grandchildren goodbye.

f.g: Here, his grandchildren and daughters.

chapters.n: Laban admits he could hurt Jacob but that Jacob’s God warned him not to. God’s protection is acknowledged even by Laban.

f.g: Last night.

chapters.n: Laban understands Jacob’s homesickness—but why steal his gods? The irony is clear: what kind of gods can be stolen?

f.g: The household idols (teraphim).

chapters.n: Jacob explains that he left secretly because he feared Laban would take his daughters by force.

f.g: Perhaps; I feared that.

chapters.n: Not knowing Rachel took the idols, Jacob rashly declares that whoever has them shall die. His words create real danger for Rachel.

f.g: A rash oath that puts Rachel at risk.

chapters.n: Laban searches every tent—Jacob’s, Leah’s, the maidservants’—and finally Rachel’s.

f.g: The tents of Bilhah and Zilpah.

chapters.n: Rachel has hidden the idols in her camel saddle and is sitting on them. Laban searches everything but finds nothing.

f.g: The camel saddle, often a basket-like seat.

chapters.n: Rachel tells her father she cannot stand because she is having her period. Laban’s precious gods are being sat upon—a mocking picture of idols.

f.g: Menstruation.
Stand respectfully in your presence.

chapters.n: Jacob angrily confronts Laban, demanding to know what crime justified such a pursuit.

f.g: Argued; quarreled (past tense of “chide”).
Wrongdoing.

chapters.n: Jacob challenges Laban to display anything he found before both families, to judge between them.

f.g: Belongings.

chapters.n: Jacob describes twenty years of faithful service: Laban’s animals did not miscarry under his care, and he never ate Laban’s rams.

f.g: Miscarried.

chapters.n: Jacob even covered the losses when wild animals killed sheep—going beyond what custom required of a shepherd.

f.g: Killed by wild animals.

chapters.n: Jacob endured burning heat by day, freezing cold by night, and lost sleep. A shepherd’s life was hard and dangerous.

f.g: Scorching heat.

f.w: my sleep departed from mine eyes

chapters.n: Twenty years: fourteen for his wives, six for flocks, with wages changed again and again.

f.w: fourteen years for thy two daughters

chapters.n: If not for God—the God of Abraham and “the Fear of Isaac”—Jacob would have left empty-handed. God saw his hardship and rebuked Laban.

f.g: A unique name for God: the One whom Isaac revered.

chapters.n: Laban claims everything is still his but admits he can do nothing. He then proposes a treaty.

f.w: all that thou seest is mine
f.g: Laban’s possessive attitude to the end.

chapters.n: Laban suggests a covenant to serve as a witness between them.

f.g: A lasting testimony of their agreement.

chapters.n: Jacob sets up a stone as a pillar, as he did at Bethel.

f.w: set it up for a pillar

chapters.n: Jacob’s relatives gather stones into a heap, and they eat a covenant meal there.

f.g: A pile of stones—a boundary marker and memorial.

chapters.n: Laban names the heap in Aramaic, and Jacob in Hebrew; both mean “heap of witness.” The two languages hint at two peoples—Arameans and Israelites.

f.g: Aramaic for “heap of witness.”
Hebrew for “heap of witness”; sounds like Gilead.

chapters.n: Laban declares the heap a witness between them.

f.g: Explains the region’s name, Gilead.

chapters.n: The place is also called Mizpah, “watchtower.” Laban’s words—“The LORD watch between me and thee”—were a warning, though today they are often used as a tender farewell.

f.g: Means “watchtower” or “lookout.”

chapters.n: Laban warns Jacob not to mistreat his daughters or marry other wives. God will be witness even when no one else is.
Laban points to the heap and pillar.

f.g: Laban claims credit for setting them up.

chapters.n: The heap and pillar mark a boundary neither will cross to harm the other—a peace treaty.

f.g: With hostile intent.

chapters.n: Laban calls on the God of Abraham and Nahor; Jacob swears by “the Fear of Isaac,” the God his father worshipped.

f.g: Laban may mean a family god distinct from Jacob’s God.

f.w: the fear of his father Isaac

chapters.n: Jacob offers a sacrifice and shares a meal with his relatives. They spend the night on the mountain.

f.g: Covenant sacrifice and meal sealed the agreement.

chapters.n: Early the next morning Laban kisses and blesses his daughters and grandchildren and goes home. Jacob is finally free to return to Canaan.

f.g: Laban exits the story for good.

chapters.n: As Jacob heads home, angels of God meet him. Angels marked his departure from Canaan at Bethel, and now they mark his return.

f.w: the angels of God met him

chapters.n: Jacob recognizes God’s army and names the place Mahanaim, “two camps”—God’s camp and his own.

f.g: God’s army or camp.
Means “two camps.” It later became a town east of the Jordan (2 Samuel 2:8).

chapters.n: Jacob sends messengers ahead to Esau, who now lives in Seir, the land of Edom. Twenty years after fleeing, Jacob must face his brother.

f.g: The mountainous region south of the Dead Sea, later Edom’s homeland.

chapters.n: Jacob instructs them to call Esau “my lord” and himself “thy servant.” Jacob humbly reverses the blessing that made him lord over his brother.

f.g: Stayed as a foreigner.

chapters.n: Jacob mentions his wealth—perhaps to show he is not coming to claim Esau’s inheritance—and seeks Esau’s favor.

f.w: that I may find grace in thy sight
f.g: That you may look on me with favor.

chapters.n: The messengers report that Esau is coming with four hundred men—an alarming number that sounds like an army.

f.g: A sizable fighting force.

chapters.n: Terrified, Jacob splits his people and animals into two camps—echoing the name Mahanaim.

f.g: Two camps, the same word as in Mahanaim.

chapters.n: If Esau attacks one camp, the other might escape. Jacob plans carefully—and then he prays.

f.w: the other company which is left shall escape
f.g: Practical preparation alongside prayer.

chapters.n: Jacob prays to the God of his fathers, reminding the Lord of His command to return and His promise to do him good. This is the first long prayer recorded in the Bible.
Jacob humbly admits he is unworthy of God’s kindness and faithfulness. He crossed the Jordan with only a staff; now he has two camps.

f.w: I am not worthy of the least of all the mercies

f.g: Hebrew ḥasadim—acts of covenant love.

chapters.n: Jacob honestly pleads for rescue from Esau, fearing for his wives and children.

f.g: An image of total destruction (compare Hosea 10:14).

chapters.n: He reminds God of His promise of countless descendants. Praying God’s promises back to Him is an act of faith.

f.w: as the sand of the sea

chapters.n: Jacob spends the night there and selects a large gift for Esau from his flocks.

f.g: Hebrew minḥah—a gift or tribute, also the word for an offering.

chapters.n: The gift is lavish: hundreds of goats and sheep.

f.g: Female sheep.

chapters.n: It also includes camels, cattle, and donkeys—over 550 animals in all, a fortune.

f.g: Camels producing milk.
Cows.

chapters.n: Jacob sends each herd separately with a gap between, so Esau will meet gift after gift.

f.g: A herd being driven.

chapters.n: He instructs the lead servant what to say when Esau asks whose animals these are.

f.g: Who is your master?

chapters.n: The servant is to say they are a gift from Esau’s servant Jacob, who is following behind.

f.g: Jacob consistently calls himself Esau’s servant.

chapters.n: Jacob gives the same instructions to every servant leading a herd.

f.g: In this way.

chapters.n: Jacob hopes to soothe Esau’s anger with gifts before seeing him face to face. The word “face” repeats through this passage, preparing for Peniel, “face of God.”

f.g: Literally “cover his face”—related to the Hebrew word for atonement (kipper).
“Face” appears several times here, building to Peniel (verse 30).

chapters.n: The gifts go ahead, and Jacob stays in the camp that night.

f.g: Spent the night.

chapters.n: That night Jacob takes his wives, maidservants, and eleven sons across the ford of the Jabbok River.

f.g: A crossing on the Jabbok River, a tributary of the Jordan. Jabbok sounds like Hebrew ’avaq, “wrestle.”
Benjamin is not yet born; Dinah is not counted here.

chapters.n: He sends everything he has across the stream.

f.g: The Jabbok stream.

chapters.n: Left alone, Jacob wrestles with a mysterious man until dawn. Jacob has struggled all his life—with Esau, with Laban—and now he wrestles with God’s messenger. Enos later describes his own “wrestle” before God in prayer.
When the man cannot overcome Jacob, he touches Jacob’s hip and dislocates it. Jacob will carry a permanent reminder of this encounter.

f.g: The hip socket.

chapters.n: The man asks to go as dawn breaks, but Jacob refuses unless he is blessed. Jacob, now weak, clings rather than fights—and seeks a blessing from God rather than by trickery.

f.w: I will not let thee go, except thou bless me

chapters.n: The man asks Jacob’s name. When Jacob last gave his name to receive a blessing, he lied (27:19). Now he answers honestly: “Jacob”—“heel-grabber.”
Jacob receives a new name: Israel, because he has striven with God and with men and prevailed. The name of a man becomes the name of a people.

f.g: Probably “God strives” or “he strives with God”; also understood as “one who prevails with God.”

f.w: as a prince hast thou power
f.g: Hebrew “you have striven.”

chapters.n: Jacob asks the man’s name but is not told. Instead, the man blesses him there.

f.w: Wherefore is it that thou dost ask after my name?

chapters.n: Jacob names the place Peniel, “face of God,” because he has seen God face to face and lived.

f.g: Means “face of God.”

f.w: I have seen God face to face

chapters.n: The sun rises as Jacob limps past Penuel. A new day dawns for a changed man.

f.g: Limped.
A variant spelling of Peniel; later a town (Judges 8:8).

chapters.n: Israelites traditionally avoid eating the thigh sinew of animals, remembering this event.

f.g: Often identified as the sciatic nerve; still avoided in Jewish dietary practice.

chapters.n: Jacob looks up and sees Esau approaching with four hundred men. He divides the children among their mothers.
Jacob arranges his family in order, with Rachel and Joseph last—the safest position. The arrangement painfully shows who he loved most.

f.g: At the very back.

chapters.n: Jacob goes ahead of his family and bows to the ground seven times—a formal gesture of humble submission, as before a king.

f.w: bowed himself to the ground seven times
f.g: Ancient court documents describe vassals bowing seven times before a king.

chapters.n: Esau runs to Jacob, embraces him, falls on his neck, and kisses him, and they both weep. Twenty years of anger melt away. Jesus’ parable of the prodigal son echoes this scene.

f.g: Threw his arms around him.

chapters.n: Esau asks who the women and children are. Jacob answers that they are gifts of God’s grace.

f.g: Given freely as a gift of grace.

chapters.n: The maidservants and their children approach and bow.

f.g: Bilhah and Zilpah.

chapters.n: Leah and her children bow next, and last Joseph and Rachel. Interestingly, Joseph is named before his mother—perhaps stepping forward to shield her.

f.w: after came Joseph near and Rachel
f.g: Joseph is mentioned first, perhaps hinting at his future prominence.

chapters.n: Esau asks about the herds he met. Jacob says they were meant to win his favor.

f.g: Herd or company.

chapters.n: Esau graciously replies that he has plenty and calls Jacob “my brother.” He does not need the gift.

f.g: Esau speaks as a brother, while Jacob keeps saying “my lord.”

chapters.n: Jacob insists, saying seeing Esau’s gracious face is like seeing the face of God. Having just met God at Peniel, Jacob now sees God’s grace in his brother’s forgiveness.

f.w: as though I had seen the face of God

chapters.n: Jacob urges Esau to accept his “blessing.” In a sense, Jacob gives back a blessing to the brother he had taken one from. Esau accepts.

f.g: Hebrew berakah—the same word for the blessing Jacob took (27:35-36).
Literally “I have everything.”

chapters.n: Esau offers to travel together, leading the way.

f.g: Esau offers to escort Jacob.

chapters.n: Jacob politely declines, explaining that the children and nursing animals cannot travel quickly. Driving them too hard would kill them—a caring shepherd’s concern.

f.g: Young and delicate.
Drive too hard.

chapters.n: Jacob suggests Esau go ahead while he follows slowly, promising to come to Seir.

f.g: Slowly; gently.
Jacob apparently never goes to Seir, perhaps wisely keeping his distance.

chapters.n: Esau offers some of his men as escort, but Jacob declines, asking only for continued goodwill.

f.g: “Why do that?”—there’s no need.

chapters.n: Esau returns that day to Seir. The brothers part in peace and later meet again to bury their father (35:29).
Jacob travels to Succoth, builds a house, and makes shelters for his animals. The name Succoth means “booths.”

f.g: Means “booths” or “shelters”; a town in the Jordan Valley (Judges 8:5).
Simple shelters, the same word as the later Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkot).

chapters.n: Jacob arrives safely at the city of Shechem in Canaan, fulfilling his vow’s hope to return in peace. He camps outside the city.

f.g: Can mean “safely” or “in peace,” or be a place name.

chapters.n: Jacob buys a plot of land from Hamor’s sons for a hundred pieces of silver. Joseph’s bones would later be buried here, and Jesus talked with a Samaritan woman nearby at “Jacob’s well.”

f.w: bought a parcel of a field

f.g: Hebrew qesitah—a unit of value of uncertain weight.

chapters.n: Jacob builds an altar and names it “El-elohe-Israel”: “God, the God of Israel.” Using his new name, Jacob declares his personal faith.

f.g: “God, the God of Israel” or “Mighty is the God of Israel.”

chapters.n: Dinah, Jacob’s daughter by Leah, goes out to visit the young women of the region. This painful chapter shows the dangers of living among the Canaanites and the family’s struggle to respond rightly to evil.

f.g: The local Canaanite women.

chapters.n: Shechem, the son of the local ruler, sees Dinah, seizes her, and rapes her. The verbs—took, lay, defiled—describe violence and humiliation.

f.g: One of the peoples of Canaan (10:17).
Humbled or violated—the Hebrew word describes forced, degrading treatment.

chapters.n: Afterward Shechem becomes attached to Dinah and speaks tenderly to her. His feelings, however, do not undo the wrong he committed.

f.g: Clung; became attached.
Literally “spoke to her heart.”

chapters.n: Shechem demands that his father obtain Dinah for him as a wife.

f.w: Get me this damsel to wife
f.g: His blunt demand mirrors his earlier taking (compare Judges 14:2).

chapters.n: Jacob hears what happened but stays silent until his sons return from the fields. His silence may be caution—or a troubling passivity.

f.g: Kept silent.

chapters.n: Hamor, Shechem’s father, comes to negotiate with Jacob.

f.g: Talk; negotiate.

chapters.n: Jacob’s sons return, grieved and furious. The narrator calls the crime an outrage “in Israel”—a disgraceful act that should never be done.

f.g: Committed a disgraceful outrage; a phrase used later for grave sexual crimes (Deuteronomy 22:21; 2 Samuel 13:12).

chapters.n: Hamor asks for Dinah as Shechem’s wife but offers no apology for the crime.

f.g: Is attached to; desires.

chapters.n: Hamor proposes broad intermarriage between the two peoples. This would have dissolved the covenant family into Canaanite society.
He offers land, trade, and property rights—an attractive offer for a wandering family.

f.g: Move about freely; do business.

chapters.n: Shechem asks for favor and promises to give whatever they ask.

f.w: Let me find grace in your eyes
f.g: Please look kindly on my request.

chapters.n: He offers to pay any bride-price and gift they name, as long as he can marry Dinah.

f.g: Bride-price paid to the bride’s family.

chapters.n: Jacob’s sons answer deceitfully because of what was done to their sister. Their response sets a trap.

f.g: With cunning or treachery; the same root used of Jacob’s earlier deceit (27:35).

chapters.n: They say they cannot give their sister to an uncircumcised man. They misuse the sacred covenant sign as a tool for revenge.

f.g: A disgrace.

chapters.n: They demand that every male in the city be circumcised as a condition.

f.w: If ye will be as we be
f.g: If you become like us.

chapters.n: If so, they promise to intermarry and become one people—a false promise.

f.g: A promise they never intend to keep.

chapters.n: Otherwise, they will take “our daughter” and go. Dinah apparently remains in Shechem’s house (verse 26).

f.g: Dinah, still held in Shechem’s house.

chapters.n: Hamor and Shechem are pleased with the terms.

f.g: Seemed good to.

chapters.n: Shechem acts without delay because of his desire for Dinah. He is described as the most respected member of his family.

f.g: Did not delay.
Most respected or influential.

chapters.n: Hamor and Shechem address the men at the city gate, where public decisions were made.

f.g: The place of public assembly and decisions.

chapters.n: They present Jacob’s family as peaceful and the land as roomy enough for everyone.

f.g: Friendly; at peace.

chapters.n: They explain the one condition: circumcision for every male.

f.g: Agree.

chapters.n: They also appeal to greed: Jacob’s wealth will become theirs. Both sides are bargaining with hidden motives.

f.w: Shall not their cattle and their substance and every beast of theirs be ours?
f.g: Hamor’s private motive revealed.

chapters.n: All the men of the city agree, and every male is circumcised.

f.w: all that went out of the gate
f.g: All the men of the city who had civic rights.

chapters.n: On the third day, while the men are in pain and weak, Simeon and Levi—Dinah’s full brothers—attack the city and kill all the males. Their revenge is far beyond justice.

f.g: In pain.

chapters.n: They kill Hamor and Shechem and take Dinah from Shechem’s house.

f.w: with the edge of the sword
f.g: With merciless violence.

chapters.n: Jacob’s other sons plunder the city, justifying it by their sister’s defilement.

f.g: Plundered; looted.

chapters.n: They take the flocks, herds, donkeys, and everything in the city and fields.

f.w: that which was in the field
f.g: Everything outside the city as well.

chapters.n: They even take the women and children captive. The wrong done to Dinah has led to far greater violence.

f.g: Children.

chapters.n: Jacob rebukes Simeon and Levi, fearing their actions have made the family hated and vulnerable to attack. His concern focuses on safety; later he condemns their violence more strongly.

f.g: To make me hated; to give me a bad reputation.

chapters.n: The brothers answer with a pointed question: should their sister be treated like a prostitute? The chapter ends without resolution, leaving readers to weigh justice, anger, and mercy.

f.g: A prostitute.

chapters.n: After the trouble at Shechem, God tells Jacob to go back to Bethel, where He first appeared to him, and build an altar. It is time for Jacob to fulfill his vow.

f.w: when thou fleddest from the face of Esau

chapters.n: Jacob calls his household to spiritual preparation: get rid of foreign idols, purify yourselves, and change clothes. Approaching God’s house requires clean hands and hearts—a principle behind temple worthiness today.

f.g: Foreign gods—perhaps including Rachel’s stolen idols and items taken from Shechem.

f.w: be clean, and change your garments

chapters.n: Jacob testifies that God answered him in his distress and stayed with him every step of the way—exactly as promised at Bethel.

f.w: was with me in the way which I went

chapters.n: The family hands over their idols and earrings, which may have been amulets. Jacob buries them under the oak near Shechem.

f.g: Possibly amulets or charms linked with idol worship.

f.w: the oak which was by Shechem

chapters.n: As they travel, a terror from God falls on the surrounding towns, so no one pursues them after the violence at Shechem. God protects the family despite its failings.

f.g: A God-sent fear or panic.

chapters.n: Jacob and his people arrive at Luz, that is, Bethel.
Jacob builds an altar and names the place El-bethel, “the God of Bethel.” His focus has shifted from the place to the God who met him there.

f.g: “God of the house of God.”

chapters.n: Deborah, Rebekah’s old nurse, dies and is buried under an oak, named the “oak of weeping.” Her presence suggests Rebekah may have died, though Scripture does not say so.

f.g: “Oak of weeping.”

chapters.n: God appears to Jacob again and blesses him, closing the circle that began at Bethel twenty years before.
God confirms Jacob’s new name, Israel. What a messenger gave at Peniel, God Himself now ratifies.
God, as El Shaddai, renews the covenant: be fruitful, become a nation and a company of nations, and kings will descend from you.

f.g: Hebrew El Shaddai.

chapters.n: God promises Jacob and his descendants the land once given to Abraham and Isaac. The covenant has now passed through three generations.

f.w: the land which I gave Abraham and Isaac

chapters.n: God “goes up” from him, a sign that this was a personal appearance.
Jacob sets up a stone pillar again and pours a drink offering and oil on it, consecrating the place.

f.g: Wine or another liquid poured out as an offering—its first mention in the Bible.

chapters.n: Jacob names the place Bethel once more. The name now carries a lifetime of meaning.

f.g: “House of God.”

chapters.n: Traveling south from Bethel, near Ephrath, Rachel goes into difficult labor.

f.g: An old name for the Bethlehem area (Micah 5:2).
Went into labor.

chapters.n: The midwife comforts Rachel: “Don’t be afraid—you have another son.” Rachel’s prayer at Joseph’s birth for another son is answered.

f.w: thou shalt have this son also

chapters.n: Dying, Rachel names her son Ben-oni, “son of my sorrow,” but Jacob renames him Benjamin, “son of the right hand”—a name of strength and honor.

f.g: “Son of my sorrow” (or “of my strength”).
“Son of the right hand,” a place of honor; or “son of the south.”

chapters.n: Rachel dies and is buried on the road to Bethlehem. Jeremiah pictures Rachel weeping for her children, and Matthew applies it to the infants of Bethlehem in Jesus’ day.

f.g: “House of bread,” later the birthplace of David and Jesus.

chapters.n: Jacob marks her grave with a pillar, still known in the narrator’s day. A traditional site of Rachel’s Tomb stands near Bethlehem today.
Israel moves on and camps beyond Migdal-eder, “the tower of the flock.”

f.g: Migdal-eder, “tower of the flock,” near Bethlehem.

chapters.n: Reuben, the firstborn, sleeps with Bilhah, his father’s secondary wife—a grave offense, perhaps an attempt to seize family leadership. It costs him the birthright, which goes to Joseph.

f.w: Reuben went and lay with Bilhah

f.g: Secondary wife.

chapters.n: Leah’s six sons are listed first: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun—future tribes of Israel.

f.g: Still listed as firstborn by birth, though he loses the birthright.

chapters.n: Rachel’s two sons: Joseph and Benjamin. Joseph will soon become the center of the story.
Bilhah’s sons: Dan and Naphtali.
Zilpah’s sons: Gad and Asher. Together the twelve sons become the twelve tribes of Israel, a pattern echoed in Christ’s Twelve Apostles.

f.w: these are the sons of Jacob

f.g: A general summary—Benjamin was actually born in Canaan.

chapters.n: Jacob finally comes home to his father Isaac at Hebron, where Abraham and Isaac had lived.

f.g: Kirjath-arba, an old name for Hebron.

chapters.n: Isaac lives to 180, the longest life of the three patriarchs.

f.g: 180 years.

chapters.n: Isaac dies full of days, and his sons Esau and Jacob bury him together—reconciled brothers honoring their father. Latter-day revelation teaches that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob have entered into their exaltation.

f.w: his sons Esau and Jacob buried him

chapters.n: A new section begins: the family record of Esau. Genesis notes that Esau is also called Edom (“red”), the name of the nation his descendants became, Israel’s neighbor to the southeast.

f.g: Hebrew “red,” recalling the red pottage Esau traded his birthright for.

chapters.n: Esau married women from the Canaanite peoples around him, something that grieved his parents Isaac and Rebekah because these wives did not share the covenant faith.
Esau also married a daughter of Ishmael, his half-uncle, apparently trying to please his father after seeing that Canaanite wives displeased him.
The first of Esau’s sons are listed by mother. Eliphaz and Reuel will become heads of important Edomite clans.

f.g: A later Eliphaz the Temanite is one of Job’s friends, perhaps from this clan.

chapters.n: Three more sons were born to Esau through Aholibamah while the family still lived in Canaan, before the move to Seir.

f.g: An Edomite chief; not the Levite Korah who later rebelled against Moses.

chapters.n: Esau gathered his whole household and herds and moved away from Jacob. The brothers had reconciled, but they lived apart.

f.g: possessions, wealth

chapters.n: Like Abraham and Lot before them, the brothers had too many flocks for the same pastureland, so they separated peacefully.

f.g: foreign residents; they lived in Canaan without owning it.

chapters.n: Esau settled in the rugged hill country of Seir, south and east of the Dead Sea, which became the land of Edom.
The record now turns to Esau’s descendants after they became a people in Seir, showing how the promise that two nations would come from Rebekah was fulfilled.
The two oldest family lines are named again as the starting point for the clan lists that follow.
Eliphaz’s sons gave their names to Edomite clans and places. Teman became a famous Edomite region known for wisdom.
Through a concubine, Eliphaz fathered Amalek, ancestor of the Amalekites who would later attack Israel in the wilderness.

f.g: a secondary wife with fewer legal rights

chapters.n: Reuel’s four sons are listed; each became the head of a clan within Edom.
Aholibamah’s sons are named again, this time to introduce them as clan leaders in the list below.
“Dukes” were tribal chiefs or clan heads, not European nobles. The leading clans descended from Eliphaz, Esau’s firstborn.

f.g: Hebrew ’alluph — chief of a clan (“a thousand”), a tribal leader.

chapters.n: More chiefs from Eliphaz’s line, including Amalek, are listed. The Edomite clans were organized by family descent.
Reuel’s sons became chiefs in Edom too, each leading a branch of Esau’s family.
Aholibamah’s three sons headed their own clans, showing all three of Esau’s wives produced leading families.
A summary line closes Esau’s own family list before turning to the earlier inhabitants of the land.
Before Esau came, Seir was home to the Horites. Their clans are listed because Esau’s family intermarried with them and eventually displaced them.

f.g: Possibly related to the Hurrians, or meaning “cave dwellers.”

chapters.n: The remaining Horite chiefs are named. These local leaders ruled Seir’s clans in the early days.
Lotan’s family is listed. His sister Timna is likely the same Timna who became the concubine of Eliphaz, linking the Horites and Edomites.
Shobal’s sons are named, more names from the local clans of Seir.
A little detail is preserved: Anah discovered something in the wilderness while herding. The Hebrew word is uncertain; many scholars read it as “hot springs” rather than mules.

f.g: Hebrew yemim, a rare word; many translations read “hot springs.”

chapters.n: Anah’s children include Aholibamah, one of Esau’s wives, showing Esau married into the leading Horite family.
Dishon’s four sons continue the Horite family record.
Ezer’s sons are named, another branch of the Horite clans.
Dishan’s sons include Uz, a name that also appears for the land where Job lived.
The Horite chiefs are listed again as rulers, parallel to the Edomite chiefs listed earlier.
This concludes the Horite leaders who governed in Seir before Edom took full control.
Edom had kings long before Israel did. This remark shows the list was recorded or updated after Israel had kings, and it recalls the promise that kings would come from Jacob.

f.w: before there reigned any king over the children of Israel

chapters.n: Bela was the first listed king. Edom’s kingship was not hereditary here—each king seems to come from a different family and city.
Jobab came from Bozrah, which became Edom’s major city and appears often in the prophets.
Husham came from Teman, the clan region named for Esau’s grandson.

f.g: the land of the Temanites

chapters.n: Hadad is remembered for a military victory over Midian in Moab, one of few personal details in the list.
Samlah of Masrekah succeeded Hadad. The kings came from different towns, suggesting a loose federation of clans.
Saul of Rehoboth (not Israel’s King Saul) reigned next. “The river” may refer to a nearby stream or even the Euphrates.
Baal-hanan’s name means “Baal is gracious,” showing Edom worshipped Canaanite gods.
The last king listed, Hadar (called Hadad in Chronicles), is the only one whose wife is named, suggesting her family was notable.
A final list names Edomite chiefs by their territories, much like a map of clan districts.

f.g: by their regions or settlements

chapters.n: More clan-districts of Edom are named, some matching names of Esau’s family members.
Kenaz and Teman appear again, now as territorial names. Caleb’s family was later linked to a Kenizzite clan.
The chapter ends by repeating that Esau is the father of the Edomites. Though not the covenant heir, Esau was blessed with a large nation, as Isaac had promised.
After the side note on Esau, the story returns to Jacob, living as a sojourner in Canaan just as Isaac had. The covenant land was promised, but not yet possessed.

f.g: a resident foreigner, living in the land without owning it

chapters.n: The long story of Joseph begins. At seventeen he worked with his half-brothers and reported their bad behavior to Jacob, which did not make him popular.

f.g: Hebrew toledot — “family history”; this one runs to the end of Genesis.
a bad account of their conduct

chapters.n: Jacob openly favored Joseph, the first son of his beloved Rachel, and gave him a special robe that marked him as the favored heir.

f.g: Hebrew ketonet passim — perhaps a long-sleeved or richly ornamented robe; a sign of rank.

chapters.n: Favoritism bred resentment. The brothers’ hatred grew so strong they could not even greet Joseph kindly—a warning about how envy poisons families.

f.g: could not even say “shalom” (peace) to him

chapters.n: Joseph shared a dream with his brothers, and it only deepened their hatred. In Genesis dreams are often a way God reveals the future.
Joseph eagerly asks them to listen. His youthful openness may have been naïve, but the dream itself was from God.

f.g: please

chapters.n: In the dream the brothers’ bundles of grain bowed to Joseph’s. Fittingly, it would be grain that later brought them to Egypt to bow before him.

f.g: bowed down in respect
bundles of cut grain

chapters.n: The brothers understood the meaning at once: Joseph would rule over them. Their questions drip with scorn, and their hatred grew.

f.w: Shalt thou indeed reign over us?

chapters.n: A second dream widened the picture: sun, moon, and eleven stars—his father, mother, and eleven brothers—bowed to him.

f.w: the sun and the moon and the eleven stars

chapters.n: Even Jacob scolded Joseph, asking whether the whole family would bow to him. The mention of “thy mother” is striking since Rachel had died; it may be symbolic of the whole household.

f.g: scolded, corrected

chapters.n: The brothers seethed with jealousy, but Jacob quietly kept the dream in mind, sensing it might mean something—much as Mary later pondered things in her heart.

f.g: kept the matter in mind

chapters.n: The brothers took the flocks about fifty miles north to Shechem, where good pasture was—and where they had earlier massacred the city’s men.
Jacob sends Joseph to check on them, and Joseph answers with readiness: “Here am I,” the same humble response of Abraham and later prophets.
Joseph is sent on a simple errand of peace—to ask after his brothers’ welfare—yet it begins his journey to Egypt. God often works through ordinary tasks.

f.w: see whether it be well with thy brethren
f.g: literally “see the shalom (peace, welfare) of your brothers”

chapters.n: A nameless man finds Joseph wandering. This small encounter keeps the story moving; without it Joseph might have gone home.
Joseph simply says he is looking for his brothers—an ironic line, since they are about to reject him.
The brothers had moved on to Dothan, about 15 miles north, along a trade route to Egypt—which sets up what happens next.

f.g: a town on the caravan road from Gilead to Egypt

chapters.n: Spotting the hated robe from far away, the brothers plotted murder before Joseph even arrived.

f.g: plotted together

chapters.n: They mock him as “this dreamer”—literally “master of dreams.” Their contempt is aimed at the very gift God gave him.

f.g: Hebrew “this lord of dreams,” a sneer

chapters.n: Their plan: kill him, hide the body in a cistern, and blame a wild animal. They intend to destroy his dreams—but they will end up fulfilling them.

f.g: a cistern dug to store rainwater

f.w: we shall see what will become of his dreams

chapters.n: Reuben, the oldest, stepped in to stop the killing. Perhaps he hoped to regain his father’s trust after his earlier sin.
Reuben proposed throwing Joseph into a dry cistern instead, secretly planning to rescue him and bring him home.
The first thing they did was strip off the robe that symbolized their father’s favor. Joseph will later be stripped of a garment again in Potiphar’s house.

f.g: stripped

chapters.n: The cistern was dry, so Joseph would not drown—but he could not climb out. Being thrown into a pit is a biblical picture of deep distress.

f.w: there was no water in it

chapters.n: Coldly, the brothers sat down to eat while Joseph cried below. A trading caravan appeared, carrying valuable resins and spices to Egypt.

f.g: Ishmaelites—traders descended from Ishmael
a healing resin; Gilead was famous for it
fragrant resin used in perfume and burial

chapters.n: Judah asks what they gain by murder. His argument is practical more than moral, but it saves Joseph’s life.
Judah suggests selling Joseph instead—“he is our brother.” It is a half-step toward conscience; Judah’s full change comes later.

f.g: our own family, our blood relative
agreed

chapters.n: Joseph was sold for twenty pieces of silver, roughly the price of a slave in that era. Christians have long seen a parallel in Jesus being sold for thirty pieces.

f.g: The trader names Ishmaelite and Midianite seem to overlap here.

chapters.n: Reuben, who had been away, came back to find the pit empty. Tearing clothing was a sign of intense grief.

f.g: tore his clothes in mourning

chapters.n: Reuben cries that the boy is gone—and as oldest son he feels responsible for facing his father.

f.g: the boy is gone

chapters.n: The brothers use a goat’s blood to fake Joseph’s death. Jacob, who once deceived his father with goat skins and Esau’s garment, is now deceived the same way.
They hand the bloody robe to Jacob and ask him to “recognize” it—a cruel way of avoiding a direct lie.

f.g: Hebrew “recognize”—a key word that returns in Genesis 38:25.

chapters.n: Jacob recognized the robe and drew the conclusion they intended: Joseph had been torn apart by a wild animal.
Jacob mourned with the customary signs: torn clothes and sackcloth, a rough goat-hair cloth worn in grief.

f.g: coarse cloth worn as a sign of mourning or repentance

chapters.n: No one could console Jacob; he expected to grieve until death. The brothers’ secret now burdens the whole family for over twenty years.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol — the world of the dead

chapters.n: Meanwhile, Joseph arrived in Egypt and was sold to Potiphar, a high royal official. The narrator hints that God’s plan is quietly unfolding.

f.g: an Egyptian name meaning roughly “he whom Ra gave”
possibly chief of the royal bodyguard or executioners

chapters.n: The story pauses Joseph’s journey to follow Judah. Judah separates from his brothers and befriends a Canaanite man from Adullam, a town in the lowlands.

f.g: from Adullam, a town in the Judean foothills

chapters.n: Judah married a Canaanite woman, the very kind of marriage Abraham and Isaac had worked to avoid for their sons.

f.g: Strictly, Shuah is her father; she is called “the daughter of Shuah.”

chapters.n: Judah’s first son is born and named Er.
A second son, Onan, is born.
A third son, Shelah, is born at Chezib. Shelah’s descendants are listed later among the clans of Judah.
